item.content:encoded:
Prospective doctoral researchers preparing for PhD study in 2027 can explore a wide range of CAM-DTP supervisor-led PhD topics for 2027 entry, covering research areas such as artificial intelligence, public health, psychology, climate change, education, biodiversity, healthcare, finance, entrepreneurship, energy governance, genomics and social research.

The CAM-DTP Studentship Opportunities for 2027 are being advertised through Route 1, the supervisor-led route. Under this pathway, prospective PhD candidates identify a research topic of interest, contact the relevant supervisory team and discuss the possibility of developing a project proposal before making a formal application.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the application procedure. CAM-DTP does not accept direct applications, and prospective candidates should not submit CVs, research proposals or other documentation directly to CAM-DTP for assessment.

Instead, candidates interested in one of the advertised PhD topics must communicate with the relevant supervisory team and subsequently apply through the CAM-DTP institution of the lead supervisor, following that university’s admissions process and applicable deadlines.

About CAM-DTP PhD Topics for 2027 Entry

The CAM-DTP has published a broad portfolio of supervisor-led PhD topics for students seeking doctoral study beginning in 2027.

The opportunities form part of Route 1, which is specifically based around projects led by supervisory teams.

This means candidates are not expected simply to submit an independent application directly to CAM-DTP. Instead, they should first identify a relevant research topic and establish communication with the supervisors connected to that project.

The available opportunities span a wide variety of disciplines and interdisciplinary research themes, making the programme relevant to prospective researchers from different academic backgrounds.

Areas represented in the 2027 list include:

  • Artificial intelligence
  • Machine learning
  • Public health
  • Healthcare
  • Psychology
  • Human behaviour
  • Climate change
  • Sustainability
  • Biodiversity
  • Education
  • Architecture
  • Entrepreneurship
  • Finance
  • Cyber resilience
  • Genomics
  • Energy governance
  • Community health
  • Social research
  • Leadership
  • Nature connection
  • Developmental research
  • Research methodology
  • Health inequalities

How the CAM-DTP Supervisor-Led Route Works

Applicants interested in one of the PhD opportunities should follow the process established by CAM-DTP.

1. Review the available PhD topics

Candidates should begin by studying the list of supervisor-led research topics available for 2027 entry.

With 39 topics listed, applicants can identify research areas that align most closely with their academic background, research experience and future doctoral interests.

2. Contact the supervisory team

Students who are interested in conducting a PhD within one of the advertised topics should contact the relevant supervisory team.

This initial communication gives prospective candidates an opportunity to find out more about the project and discuss the development of a possible research proposal.

3. Speak to the supervisory team before applying

CAM-DTP specifically states that an application to conduct a PhD within one of the advertised topics should not be made before speaking to the supervisory team.

Candidates should therefore treat contact with the relevant supervisors as an essential part of the application process.

4. Apply through the lead supervisor’s institution

Once a candidate has discussed the opportunity with the supervisory team, the formal application should be made to the CAM-DTP institution where the lead supervisor is based.

Applicants must follow the admissions procedures and deadlines set by that institution.

5. Interview stage

Supervisory teams will interview candidates who are interested in their respective research topics.

The interview process provides the supervisory team with an opportunity to assess prospective candidates before determining whom to put forward for nomination.

6. CAM-DTP nomination

Following the interview process, supervisory teams will propose selected candidates to their departments for CAM-DTP nomination in early February.

Candidates should therefore begin engaging with supervisors and institutional admissions processes well before this nomination stage.

Important: CAM-DTP Does Not Accept Direct Applications

Prospective candidates should note that CAM-DTP does not take direct applications.

Applicants should therefore not send:

  • Research proposals directly to CAM-DTP
  • CVs directly to CAM-DTP
  • Supporting documentation directly to CAM-DTP
  • General PhD applications directly to CAM-DTP for review

The appropriate process is to contact the supervisory team associated with the chosen research topic and subsequently apply through the lead supervisor’s institution.

List of CAM-DTP Supervisor-Led PhD Topics for 2027

The 2027 Route 1 opportunities include 39 supervisor-led research topics.

1. The Role of Culture in Human Biological Evolution

This topic examines the relationship between culture and human biological evolution.

2. Applying Eye-Tracking in Architectural Design

This opportunity focuses on the use of eye-tracking in the context of architectural design.

3. Making Climate Messaging Work: Multimodal Insights

This research topic focuses on climate messaging and multimodal approaches.

4. Active Roots: Youth Moving for Nature & Health

This project brings together themes relating to young people, nature and health.

5. Pregnant Women’s Adaptation to Climate Change

This research topic focuses on how pregnant women adapt to challenges associated with climate change.

6. Conspiratorial Thinking in Adolescence

This PhD opportunity explores conspiratorial thinking among adolescents.

7. AI and Inclusive Entrepreneurial Ecosystems

This project examines artificial intelligence in relation to inclusive entrepreneurial ecosystems.

8. PRME and Net Zero Transition Using AI Apps

This research topic connects artificial intelligence applications with the transition towards net zero.

9. AI in Radiology Departments: Opportunity or Threat

This project examines the role and implications of artificial intelligence within radiology departments.

10. Rethinking Evidence Synthesis for Public Health

This opportunity focuses on evidence synthesis methodologies within public health.

11. AI, Machine Learning and the Future of Finance

This topic explores artificial intelligence, machine learning and their relationship with the future of finance.

12. Shared Decision-Making Protocol for Therapeutic Gaming

This research opportunity considers shared decision-making in connection with therapeutic gaming.

13. Inclusive Practices for Lab-Based Education

This project focuses on inclusive practices within laboratory-based education.

14. Health and Activity Impacts of Evolving Cities

This topic explores health and physical activity in the context of changing urban environments.

15. Causal Inference in Developmental Psychology

This PhD topic brings together causal inference methods and developmental psychology.

16. Social Acceptability of Biodiversity-Friendly Grassland Management

This project examines the social acceptability of approaches designed to support biodiversity-friendly grassland management.

17. From Clinic to Community: Autism Screening in Infancy

This opportunity focuses on autism screening in infancy and its movement from clinical to community contexts.

18. Cultivating Fungal Literacy in Gardens

This project focuses on fungal literacy in garden environments.

19. Zoo Spaces and Equitable Nature Connection

This research topic explores zoo spaces in relation to equitable connections with nature.

20. AI-Assisted Methodology for Social Survey Research

This opportunity examines how artificial intelligence can be applied to social survey research methodology.

21. Cognitive Rehabilitation Pathways Post-Stroke

This project focuses on pathways for cognitive rehabilitation following stroke.

22. Paediatric Genomics and Family Well-Being

This topic examines paediatric genomics in relation to the well-being of families.

23. Impact Evaluation of the Cambridge Science Centre

This research opportunity centres on evaluating the impact of the Cambridge Science Centre.

24. Health Insights from 19th–20th Century Vaccination Registers

This PhD topic focuses on deriving health-related insights from historical vaccination registers.

25. Psychology of Unethical Decisions and Public Trust

This research topic examines the psychology of unethical decision-making and its relationship with public trust.

26. Culture & Leadership in Transnational CPD

This opportunity investigates culture and leadership in transnational continuing professional development.

27. Personalised Behavioural Cyber Resilience

This research topic brings together behavioural approaches and cyber resilience.

28. Working with Increasingly Capable AI Agents

This project examines issues associated with working alongside increasingly capable artificial intelligence agents.

29. Adaptive AI to Reduce Neurodivergent Inequalities

This topic explores adaptive artificial intelligence in relation to inequalities affecting neurodivergent people.

30. Trauma-Informed Practices in Higher Education

This research opportunity focuses on trauma-informed approaches within higher education.

31. Help or Harm? AI in Health Emergency Preparedness

This project examines artificial intelligence in relation to health emergency preparedness.

32. Transition Expertise in Energy Governance

This research topic focuses on transition expertise within energy governance.

33. Workplace Action to Tackle Smoking Inequalities

This opportunity examines workplace-based approaches to addressing smoking inequalities.

34. Fairer Cognitive Assessment in Homeless Healthcare

This research topic focuses on improving fairness in cognitive assessment within healthcare for people experiencing homelessness.

35. United Communities, Healthier Men

This project centres on the relationship between communities and men’s health.

36. Supporting Those Close to People Who Hoard

This topic focuses on support for individuals who are close to people who hoard.

37. Betting Machines: AI in Prediction Markets

This research project explores artificial intelligence in relation to prediction markets.

38. Can AI Be Persuaded the Wrong Way?

This project examines questions relating to persuasion and artificial intelligence.

39. Inclusive Enterprise for Displaced Communities

This topic focuses on inclusive enterprise in relation to displaced communities.

Research Areas Represented in the 2027 Opportunities

The CAM-DTP 2027 portfolio demonstrates a particularly broad interdisciplinary scope.

Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology

A significant number of the projects relate to artificial intelligence and its growing influence across different areas.

These include:

  • AI and Inclusive Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
  • PRME and Net Zero Transition Using AI Apps
  • AI in Radiology Departments: Opportunity or Threat
  • AI, Machine Learning and the Future of Finance
  • AI-Assisted Methodology for Social Survey Research
  • Working with Increasingly Capable AI Agents
  • Adaptive AI to Reduce Neurodivergent Inequalities
  • Help or Harm? AI in Health Emergency Preparedness
  • Betting Machines: AI in Prediction Markets
  • Can AI Be Persuaded the Wrong Way?

These opportunities demonstrate how AI-related research is being connected to healthcare, finance, entrepreneurship, sustainability, inclusion and social research.

Public Health and Healthcare

Several available projects focus on public health, healthcare and well-being.

Relevant topics include:

  • Pregnant Women’s Adaptation to Climate Change
  • Rethinking Evidence Synthesis for Public Health
  • Health and Activity Impacts of Evolving Cities
  • From Clinic to Community: Autism Screening in Infancy
  • Cognitive Rehabilitation Pathways Post-Stroke
  • Paediatric Genomics and Family Well-Being
  • Health Insights from 19th–20th Century Vaccination Registers
  • Workplace Action to Tackle Smoking Inequalities
  • Fairer Cognitive Assessment in Homeless Healthcare
  • United Communities, Healthier Men

Climate, Nature and Environmental Research

Candidates interested in environmental research can also explore topics connected with climate change, biodiversity and relationships with nature.

These include:

  • Making Climate Messaging Work: Multimodal Insights
  • Active Roots: Youth Moving for Nature & Health
  • Pregnant Women’s Adaptation to Climate Change
  • Social Acceptability of Biodiversity-Friendly Grassland Management
  • Cultivating Fungal Literacy in Gardens
  • Zoo Spaces and Equitable Nature Connection
  • Transition Expertise in Energy Governance

Psychology, Behaviour and Society

A number of projects also address human behaviour, psychological processes and societal challenges.

Examples include:

  • Conspiratorial Thinking in Adolescence
  • Causal Inference in Developmental Psychology
  • Psychology of Unethical Decisions and Public Trust
  • Personalised Behavioural Cyber Resilience
  • Supporting Those Close to People Who Hoard

Education and Learning

Candidates interested in education may find opportunities such as:

  • Inclusive Practices for Lab-Based Education
  • Culture & Leadership in Transnational CPD
  • Trauma-Informed Practices in Higher Education

CAM-DTP Participating Universities Highlighted on the Opportunity Page

The CAM-DTP opportunity page directs candidates to information about research degrees at several universities.

These include:

  • Anglia Ruskin University
  • University of Bedfordshire
  • University of Cambridge

The institution to which an applicant formally applies will depend on where the lead supervisor associated with the chosen research topic is based.

Applicants should therefore check the relevant institutional admissions requirements carefully after discussing the project with the supervisory team.

Application Deadline for CAM-DTP PhD Topics 2027

There is no single universal application deadline stated on the supplied CAM-DTP opportunity page.

Applicants are instructed to follow the admissions process and deadlines established by the institution of the lead supervisor.

The CAM-DTP information does, however, state that supervisory teams will interview candidates and propose candidates to their departments for CAM-DTP nomination in early February.

Prospective students should therefore contact supervisors as early as possible rather than waiting until close to the nomination period.

How to Apply

Candidates interested in the CAM-DTP PhD opportunities for 2027 should follow these steps:

  1. Visit the official CAM-DTP Studentship Opportunities page.
  2. Review the complete list of supervisor-led topics.
  3. Identify the research topic that best aligns with your academic and research interests.
  4. Contact the relevant supervisory team.
  5. Discuss the research topic and possible project proposal.
  6. Do not formally apply before communicating with the supervisory team.
  7. Determine which CAM-DTP institution hosts the lead supervisor.
  8. Review that institution’s postgraduate admissions requirements and deadline.
  9. Submit the formal PhD application through the relevant university.
  10. Participate in the supervisory team’s interview process if invited.
  11. Successful candidates may then be put forward by the supervisory team for departmental CAM-DTP nomination.

APPLY NOW

Official CAM-DTP Opportunity Page

Prospective applicants should use the official CAM-DTP website to review the opportunities and obtain the latest information about individual projects and supervisory teams:

https://www.cam-dtp.ac.uk/students/current-opportunities/

Important Advice for Prospective Applicants

Because these are supervisor-led projects, selecting a topic should involve more than simply choosing an appealing project title.

Candidates should carefully consider whether a project is aligned with their:

  • Previous academic study
  • Research experience
  • Methodological skills
  • Subject interests
  • Career ambitions
  • Intended area of doctoral specialisation

Prospective applicants should also use their initial communication with supervisors to gain a clearer understanding of the project before beginning a formal application.

Candidates should not assume that the same application deadline, academic requirement or admissions process applies to every project, because applications are submitted through the institution associated with each lead supervisor.

Conclusion

The CAM-DTP PhD Studentship Opportunities for 2027 entry provide prospective doctoral researchers with access to 39 supervisor-led research topics spanning some of today’s most significant academic and societal issues.

From artificial intelligence and machine learning to healthcare, psychology, climate change, biodiversity, education, finance, energy governance, entrepreneurship and social inclusion, the breadth of the available topics creates opportunities for researchers interested in a wide range of interdisciplinary fields.

The most important part of the application process is understanding that CAM-DTP does not accept direct applications.

Prospective candidates must first select a research topic, contact the relevant supervisory team and discuss their proposed PhD project. They should then apply through the CAM-DTP institution of the lead supervisor and comply with that institution’s individual admissions procedures and deadlines.

With supervisory teams expected to put forward candidates for departmental CAM-DTP nomination in early February, prospective applicants interested in 2027 entry should explore the available topics and begin contacting relevant supervisors well in advance.

item.content:encoded:
The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA/ECA) Continental Call for African AI Innovations 2026 is now open, offering African innovators an opportunity to showcase practical artificial intelligence solutions addressing some of the continent’s most pressing development challenges.

The call will identify promising African-led, AI-enabled innovations for participation in the ECA Innovation Café, which will take place as part of the 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum (AfIGF 2026) from 2–5 November 2026 in Accra, Ghana.

Organised by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) through the Africa IGF Secretariat, in collaboration with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and Research ICT Africa (RIA), the initiative seeks to move discussions about artificial intelligence beyond its future potential and towards the practical solutions that African innovators are already developing and implementing.

African startups, technology companies, universities, researchers, innovation hubs, public institutions, private-sector organisations, social enterprises, individual innovators and innovation teams with functioning AI-enabled solutions are encouraged to apply.

The application deadline is 2 October 2026. While the main AfIGF opportunity page currently does not display the deadline in its body, the 2 October deadline is listed by the Ghana AI Summit opportunity directory and has also been publicised in posts associated with the Africa IGF call.

About the ECA Innovation Café at AfIGF 2026

The ECA Innovation Café is being organised under the theme:

“Bridging Policy, Innovation and Implementation through African AI-Enabled Solutions.”

It will form part of the 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum, scheduled to take place in Accra, Ghana, from 2–5 November 2026.

The broader AfIGF 2026 brings together stakeholders involved in Africa’s rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, including policymakers, regulators, researchers, academia, civil society, private-sector representatives, members of the technical community, youth leaders, international organisations and development partners.

For the Innovation Café specifically, ECA is seeking African innovators who are not simply proposing theoretical uses of artificial intelligence but are already developing practical solutions capable of addressing real development needs.

The initiative recognises that innovation is already taking place throughout Africa. Startups, universities, research institutions, technology hubs, public-sector organisations, companies and independent innovators are building technologies designed around African realities and priorities.

The ECA Innovation Café will provide a continental platform through which some of these solutions can be presented, discussed and connected with stakeholders who may help create the conditions necessary for responsible deployment, wider adoption and sustainable growth.

Why UNECA Is Calling for African AI Innovations

Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important component of Africa’s digital transformation.

However, the ECA Innovation Café is intended to move the conversation beyond simply asking what artificial intelligence might eventually accomplish for the continent.

Instead, the programme will focus on a more immediate question: What are African innovators already doing with AI to solve real problems?

The initiative will therefore highlight existing African-led innovations, including:

  • The solutions innovators are currently developing;
  • The development problems these solutions seek to address;
  • Results or potential impact demonstrated by the innovations;
  • Challenges innovators encounter when developing or deploying their technologies;
  • Barriers preventing promising solutions from achieving wider adoption;
  • Policy and regulatory conditions affecting AI innovation;
  • Support required by innovators;
  • Opportunities for collaboration and investment; and
  • Conditions required to scale responsible AI solutions sustainably.

This practical orientation creates an opportunity to bring technology development and policymaking closer together.

What Types of AI Innovations Are Being Sought?

Applicants should be developing practical, AI-enabled solutions addressing development challenges in Africa.

ECA highlights several areas in which African innovators are already applying technology to respond to local needs and development priorities.

1. Health

AI-enabled health innovations could help strengthen healthcare delivery, diagnostics, health information systems, disease monitoring, access to services and other areas of public health.

Innovators developing technologies that respond to healthcare challenges within African communities may therefore be relevant to the call.

2. Agriculture

Agriculture remains central to livelihoods and economic development across much of Africa.

AI-enabled solutions could contribute to areas such as agricultural productivity, information services, crop management, market access, resource management and decision-making for farmers and agricultural businesses.

3. Education

Technology and artificial intelligence can potentially help address educational challenges through digital learning, educational tools, personalised learning, improved access to information and other innovations.

Solutions demonstrating practical applications of AI within education may be considered.

4. Financial Inclusion

The call also recognises financial inclusion as an important area for innovation.

African innovators using AI to improve access to financial services or develop solutions addressing financial barriers affecting individuals, communities or businesses may have relevant innovations to submit.

5. Climate Action

Climate-related challenges require solutions that respond to environmental and economic realities across the continent.

AI-enabled innovations contributing to climate action, environmental resilience or related development priorities are among the areas highlighted by ECA.

6. Public-Service Delivery

Governments and public institutions increasingly use digital technologies to improve the way services are delivered.

Innovations that use AI to strengthen public services, improve accessibility, increase efficiency or address challenges faced by communities may therefore fit within the programme.

7. Trade

Artificial intelligence can also be applied to challenges associated with trade, commerce and economic participation.

The Innovation Café provides scope for innovators developing solutions capable of supporting Africa’s trade and broader development priorities.

8. Small-Business Development

Small and growing businesses are critical components of African economies.

AI-enabled technologies that help entrepreneurs and small businesses improve operations, access opportunities, overcome market barriers or strengthen their competitiveness may also fall within the areas targeted by the initiative.

These areas are examples rather than an indication that every eligible innovation must fit narrowly within one particular sector. The central requirement is that applicants demonstrate a practical AI-enabled solution responding to an African development challenge.

The Connection to the Sustainable Development Goals and Agenda 2063

The ECA Innovation Café is also intended to highlight African-led AI solutions contributing to broader continental and international development objectives.

In particular, selected solutions should demonstrate relevance to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the African Union’s Agenda 2063.

This places the programme within a broader conversation about how technology can contribute to sustainable development rather than being developed independently of social, economic and public-policy priorities.

The emphasis is therefore not simply on technological sophistication.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate how their innovation addresses a meaningful challenge or has credible potential to generate development impact.

Two Major Components of the ECA Innovation Café

Selected innovators will participate in an initiative built around two complementary components: the Innovation-to-Policy Exchange and the Innovation Exhibition.

1. Innovation-to-Policy Exchange

The Innovation-to-Policy Exchange will provide selected innovators with an opportunity to present their solutions and interact directly with important stakeholders.

This is particularly significant because technological solutions do not operate in isolation. Their ability to scale can depend on policies, regulations, investment, partnerships, infrastructure and wider institutional support.

Through the exchange, innovators will have an opportunity to engage with stakeholders such as:

  • Policymakers;
  • Development partners;
  • Investors;
  • Researchers;
  • Private-sector representatives;
  • Technical experts; and
  • Other actors involved in Africa’s innovation and digital-development ecosystem.

The exchange is intended to help bridge the gap between developing an innovation and creating the conditions required for that innovation to be implemented, adopted and scaled.

2. Innovation Exhibition

The second component is the Innovation Exhibition.

Selected innovations will be showcased during AfIGF 2026, giving participating innovators a platform to demonstrate their solutions within a major continental forum focused on digital governance and development.

The exhibition can provide visibility for technologies that are already moving beyond the idea stage and demonstrate how African innovators are using artificial intelligence to respond to practical challenges.

An Opportunity to Connect Innovation With Policy

One of the defining features of the ECA Innovation Café is its focus on the relationship between innovation, policy and implementation.

A promising technological solution may still face substantial barriers before it can reach the communities, institutions or markets that could benefit from it.

Those barriers can include regulatory challenges, insufficient funding, infrastructure constraints, limited institutional partnerships, difficulties entering new markets or a lack of opportunities to engage directly with decision-makers.

The Innovation Café seeks to create a space where these issues can be discussed alongside the technology itself.

By bringing innovators into direct contact with policymakers, investors, development organisations, researchers, companies and technical stakeholders, the initiative can help generate a more practical discussion around what African AI innovators need to deploy their technologies responsibly and scale them sustainably.

Who Can Apply for the UNECA Continental Call for African AI Innovations?

The opportunity is open to a broad range of innovators and organisations working within Africa’s technology, research, public-policy and development ecosystems.

Eligible applicants include:

  1. African startups and technology companies developing AI-enabled products, platforms or services;
  2. Universities and research institutions developing practical AI applications or translating research into usable solutions;
  3. Innovation hubs and laboratories supporting or developing technology-based solutions;
  4. Private-sector organisations working on AI-enabled approaches to development challenges;
  5. Public institutions and public-sector innovation teams developing technology to improve services or respond to public needs;
  6. Social enterprises combining technology and social impact;
  7. Individual innovators developing eligible solutions; and
  8. Innovation teams working collaboratively on AI-enabled technologies.

This broad eligibility reflects the reality that significant technological innovation can emerge from many different environments, not only established technology companies.

What Stage Should Your Innovation Have Reached?

An important eligibility condition is that applicants should have progressed beyond an idea alone.

Applicants are expected to demonstrate one of the following:

  • A functioning prototype;
  • A pilot; or
  • A deployed solution.

In addition, the innovation should be supported by either evidence of development impact or a credible potential to generate meaningful impact.

This means applicants should be prepared to demonstrate not only what their technology does, but also why the solution matters and how it could contribute to addressing an identifiable development challenge.

What Could Strengthen an Application?

Based on the published requirements and objectives of the Innovation Café, applicants should ensure that their submission clearly explains the practical nature of their innovation.

A strong application should make it easy to understand:

  • The specific development challenge being addressed;
  • Why that challenge matters within an African context;
  • How artificial intelligence is incorporated into the solution;
  • Who the intended users or beneficiaries are;
  • The current stage of the technology;
  • Whether a functioning prototype, pilot or deployed product currently exists;
  • Any results or evidence generated so far;
  • The actual or potential development impact;
  • Challenges affecting implementation or scale;
  • Why engagement with policymakers and other stakeholders would be valuable; and
  • How the innovation could potentially achieve wider adoption.

Applicants should rely on verifiable evidence wherever possible rather than making broad claims about potential impact.

Why the ECA Innovation Café Matters for African Innovators

Africa’s AI ecosystem is expanding across universities, research organisations, startups, public institutions, innovation hubs and businesses.

Yet developing a promising technology is only one part of creating lasting impact.

Innovators may also need supportive public policy, investment, institutional partnerships, market access, technical networks and opportunities to demonstrate their solutions to decision-makers.

The Innovation Café is designed to bring these different parts of the ecosystem together.

Rather than treating innovation and policymaking as separate conversations, the initiative seeks to create direct interaction between those building technologies and those influencing the environments in which those technologies will operate.

About the Africa Internet Governance Forum 2026

The 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum (AfIGF 2026) will take place in Accra, Ghana, from 2–5 November 2026.

The Forum’s overarching theme is:

“Advancing Africa’s Digital Future Through Innovation, Inclusion, and Trust.”

AfIGF 2026 will bring together a diverse range of participants, including policymakers, regulators, civil society, academia, technical experts, private-sector stakeholders, youth leaders, parliamentarians, members of the judiciary and international organisations.

The Forum is expected to address major issues affecting Africa’s digital future, including artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, digital inclusion, cybersecurity, digital trust, human rights, online safety, digital public infrastructure, climate change and technology, and digital sovereignty.

The ECA Innovation Café therefore places selected innovators within a wider continental conversation about how Africa can develop an innovative, inclusive and trusted digital ecosystem.

ECA Innovation Café 2026 Event Details

Applicants should note the following key information:

  • Event: ECA Innovation Café at the 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum (AfIGF 2026)
  • Theme: Bridging Policy, Innovation and Implementation through African AI-Enabled Solutions
  • Dates: 2–5 November 2026
  • Location: Accra, Ghana
  • Organiser: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa through the Africa IGF Secretariat
  • Collaborating organisations: International Telecommunication Union and Research ICT Africa
  • Application deadline: 2 October 2026

How to Apply for the UNECA Continental Call for African AI Innovations 2026

Eligible African innovators and organisations interested in participating should submit their application through the official application form provided for the ECA Innovation Café.

Applicants should prepare sufficient information about their AI-enabled innovation, its stage of development and the development challenge it addresses.

Most importantly, applicants should be able to demonstrate that they have a functioning prototype, pilot or deployed solution, rather than an idea that has not yet reached a demonstrable stage. They should also provide evidence of development impact or demonstrate credible potential for meaningful impact.

Applications can be submitted through the official application form:

Application Form: https://forms.gle/aRdJT7Renr1fNECk7

Further information about the opportunity is available through the Africa Internet Governance Forum:

Official Opportunity Page: https://igf.africa/ecainnovationcafe/

For enquiries about the ECA Innovation Café, applicants can contact:

Email: sorene@un.org

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the ECA Innovation Café at AfIGF 2026 is 2 October 2026.

Interested innovators are encouraged to prepare their submissions early enough to clearly explain their solution, demonstrate its current stage of development and provide credible evidence supporting its potential or existing development impact.

Conclusion

The UNECA Continental Call for African AI Innovations 2026 provides an important platform for innovators who are already translating artificial intelligence into practical solutions for Africa’s development challenges.

Through the ECA Innovation Café at the 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum, selected innovators will have an opportunity to move beyond simply presenting technology and participate in a broader conversation involving policy, implementation, responsible adoption and sustainable scale.

Whether an AI-enabled solution is addressing healthcare, agriculture, education, financial inclusion, climate action, public services, trade, small-business development or another significant African development challenge, the initiative offers a platform for demonstrating how home-grown innovation can contribute to Africa’s digital and sustainable-development ambitions.

For startups, universities, researchers, innovation hubs, companies, public institutions, social enterprises and independent innovators with a functioning prototype, pilot or deployed AI-enabled solution, this continental call represents an opportunity to bring practical African innovation into direct dialogue with policymakers, investors, development partners, researchers and the wider technical community.

Applications should be submitted by 2 October 2026, ahead of the ECA Innovation Café and AfIGF 2026 taking place from 2–5 November 2026 in Accra, Ghana.

Visit the OFY website for more Competition Opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
Young people with lived experience of migration and displacement are being invited to take part in the Migration Youth and Children Platform (MYCP) Policy Lab, an online programme designed to bring youth perspectives into international discussions surrounding climate change, migration, artificial intelligence, labour policy and the future of work.

Under the theme “Climate, Migration, AI & the Future of Work,” the MYCP Policy Lab brings together young people from around the world to learn directly from policymakers, international experts and practitioners while developing practical policy recommendations.

The programme is particularly focused on a major global challenge: as climate change transforms economies, livelihoods and patterns of human mobility, young migrants are among those directly affected by changing labour markets and climate-related displacement, yet their perspectives are often underrepresented in the development of policies that affect them.

Through the Policy Lab, participants will have an opportunity to move beyond simply discussing these challenges. They will work collaboratively to develop a policy brief focused on climate-labour policy and migrant youth inclusion, with the strongest work contributing to MYCP’s international advocacy.

The programme is delivered entirely online, opening participation to eligible young people from around the world.

About the MYCP Policy Lab

The MYCP Policy Lab is an interactive youth policy programme developed by the Migration Youth and Children Platform (MYCP).

Rather than functioning only as a series of lectures or presentations, the Policy Lab combines learning, discussion, teamwork and policy development.

Participants will engage with experts and other young people before working in teams to translate what they have learned into concrete policy recommendations.

The programme brings young participants into conversations with high-level policymakers and experts, including individuals with experience across international organisations, the United Nations system, the World Bank, academia, medicine and advocacy.

Through this combination of expert knowledge and youth experience, MYCP aims to create an environment where young migrants can contribute meaningfully to discussions that influence international migration and climate policy.

Why Climate Change, Migration and the Future of Work Matter

Climate change is not only an environmental challenge. Its consequences extend into employment, migration, health, education, gender equality and economic opportunity.

Changes in climate conditions can affect where people are able to live, which industries can provide sustainable employment and what types of jobs will exist in the future.

For migrants and young people on the move, these transformations can create additional challenges.

Climate-related disruption can contribute to displacement and migration, while changes in economies and labour markets can determine whether young migrants have access to secure and inclusive employment opportunities.

At the same time, emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, are transforming the nature of work.

The MYCP Policy Lab places young migrants within this wider conversation about climate, migration, AI and employment, giving participants an opportunity to examine these interconnected issues and contribute ideas for more inclusive policies.

What Participants Will Do During the MYCP Policy Lab

A major component of the programme is collaborative policy development.

Participants will work in teams to develop a policy brief addressing climate-labour policy and migrant youth inclusion.

This provides participants with an opportunity to apply what they learn during the expert sessions and discussions to a practical policy-making exercise.

Instead of simply learning about international policy processes, participants will experience elements of the policy-development process themselves.

Teams will explore challenges, discuss potential solutions and formulate recommendations that can contribute to broader advocacy surrounding migrant youth.

The programme culminates in final team presentations before a jury.

The winning policy brief will be published on the MYCP website and incorporated into MYCP’s advocacy for COP31, providing an avenue for participants’ ideas to reach broader international policy discussions.

What Participants Will Gain

Participation in the MYCP Policy Lab offers several learning, professional development and networking opportunities.

1. Expert Insights Into Climate, Labour and Migration

Participants will explore the relationship between climate change, employment and migration through perspectives provided by international organisations, activists and practitioners.

This can help young people understand how these issues intersect and how policies in one area may influence outcomes in another.

2. Perspectives Across Health, Gender and Education

The programme takes an intersectional approach rather than examining migration solely as an isolated policy issue.

Participants can expect perspectives relating to areas including:

  • Health
  • Gender
  • Education
  • Migration
  • Climate change
  • Labour and employment
  • Youth inclusion
  • International policy development

MYCP states that perspectives will include specialists associated with organisations such as UN Women, the World Bank and the International Labour Organization (ILO).

3. Practical Policy Development Experience

Participants will have the opportunity to work directly on the development of a policy brief.

This provides practical exposure to activities such as identifying policy challenges, working collaboratively, considering evidence and developing recommendations.

For young people interested in international relations, migration, sustainable development, advocacy or public policy, this can provide valuable introductory experience in policy development.

4. Certificate of Participation

Participants will receive a certificate of participation.

The certificate can serve as formal recognition of involvement in the programme and may be included on a participant’s CV or professional profile.

5. International Youth Network

Another significant aspect of the programme is the opportunity to connect with young people from different parts of the world who share an interest in migration and international policy.

Participants can build relationships with peers who are interested in contributing to migration policy, youth advocacy and international development.

6. Opportunity to Contribute to COP31 Advocacy

The programme is designed to lead to a tangible policy output.

The winning team’s policy brief will be published by MYCP and used as part of the organisation’s advocacy for COP31.

This gives participants an opportunity to contribute ideas that may form part of wider advocacy concerning climate change, labour and migrant youth inclusion.

MYCP Policy Lab Programme Schedule

The Policy Lab is structured around two principal days of online activities followed by separate final presentations.

Day 1: Introduction, Policymaking and Intersectional Approaches

The first day of the Policy Lab is scheduled to include:

  • An introduction to the Migration Youth and Children Platform
  • An introduction to the Policy Lab and its objectives
  • Exploration of the policymaking process from the perspective of international organisations
  • Discussion of community policy programmes
  • Examination of intersectional approaches to policy

This opening day is designed to provide participants with foundational knowledge that they can use during the collaborative policy-development process.

Day 2: Thematic Learning and Policy Brief Development

The second day moves further into thematic discussions and practical teamwork.

Activities are expected to include:

  • Thematic sessions addressing health, gender and education
  • Team breakout sessions
  • Collaborative policy brief development
  • Discussion of prizes
  • Information about next steps following the Lab

The team breakout sessions will provide participants with an opportunity to collaborate directly with other young people and begin translating discussions from the programme into policy recommendations.

Final Presentations

Following the two main Policy Lab days, teams will participate in final presentations.

According to MYCP, the presentations are scheduled for 17 or 18 October, with the final date to be confirmed.

During the final stage:

  • Participating teams will present their work before a jury.
  • Teams will showcase their policy proposals and recommendations.
  • A winning policy brief will be selected.
  • The winning brief will contribute to MYCP’s COP31 advocacy.

This final presentation stage adds a practical dimension to the programme by requiring participants to communicate and defend the ideas developed through their collaborative work.

Who Can Apply for the MYCP Policy Lab?

The opportunity is intended for young people on the move from anywhere in the world.

MYCP particularly encourages participation from young people with lived experience of climate migration.

Importantly, applicants are not required to have an established background in public policy.

According to MYCP, no previous policy experience is required. The organisation emphasises curiosity and commitment as sufficient foundations for participating in the programme.

This makes the Policy Lab potentially accessible to young people from a variety of educational, professional and personal backgrounds.

Applicants may therefore be interested in areas such as migration, climate change, youth advocacy, sustainable development, international relations, public policy, human rights, education, gender equality, health or the future of work without necessarily having formal qualifications in those fields.

Is Previous Policy Experience Required?

No formal policy background is listed as a requirement for participation.

This is an important feature of the MYCP Policy Lab because policy opportunities can sometimes appear inaccessible to young people without academic or professional experience in government, international relations or public policy.

MYCP instead describes curiosity and commitment as sufficient.

Participants will learn about policymaking during the programme and then have the opportunity to apply that knowledge through collaborative policy brief development.

Is the MYCP Policy Lab Open Internationally?

Yes. MYCP describes the programme as being for young people on the move from anywhere in the world.

The online format further supports international participation by removing the requirement to travel to a physical venue.

Applicants should nevertheless review the official application form and programme information carefully for any additional participation requirements, scheduling considerations or eligibility conditions.

About the Migration Youth and Children Platform

The Migration Youth and Children Platform (MYCP) works to increase the participation of children and young people in international migration policymaking.

MYCP operates by, with and for children and young people on the move and forms part of the Major Group for Children and Youth (MGCY).

MGCY serves as an official, formal and self-organised space through which children and young people under the age of 30 can contribute to and engage in certain United Nations intergovernmental and related policy processes.

MYCP’s broader mission is to bridge the gap between children and youth and the United Nations system, particularly on migration-related issues.

The organisation seeks to promote meaningful youth participation across four major areas:

  1. Policy and Advocacy – supporting youth engagement with migration and sustainable development policymaking.
  2. Capacity Building – helping children and young people develop the knowledge and capabilities necessary to participate effectively.
  3. Youth Action – supporting youth-led engagement and initiatives.
  4. Knowledge – strengthening access to information, research and knowledge relevant to children, youth and migration.

Through these areas of work, MYCP aims to ensure that young people affected by migration are not simply discussed within international policy processes but have opportunities to participate in them.

MYCP Policy Lab Dates and Format

The official MYCP webpage currently lists the following programme information:

  • Format: Online
  • Policy Lab: 10–11 October 2025
  • Final presentations: 17 or 18 October, with the final date to be confirmed
  • Application status displayed by MYCP: Applications open now

Prospective applicants should note that there is an apparent date inconsistency on the official webpage. Although the page currently states that applications are open, it lists the Policy Lab dates as 10–11 October 2025. Applicants are therefore strongly advised to verify the applicable programme year and dates directly with MYCP before applying.

Application Deadline

No specific application deadline is currently stated on the official MYCP Policy Lab webpage.

The page states that applications are open now, but does not provide a closing date.

Because the published programme dates and current application status appear inconsistent, prospective applicants should check the official MYCP website or application form for the latest information before submitting an application.

How to Apply for the MYCP Policy Lab

Interested candidates can apply online through the application form available on the official MYCP Policy Lab webpage.

Applicants should:

  1. Visit the official MYCP Policy Lab webpage.
  2. Review the programme information and eligibility criteria.
  3. Navigate to the Apply Now section.
  4. Open the online application form.
  5. Complete all required information carefully.
  6. Review the information provided before submission.
  7. Submit the application according to the instructions in the form.

Because no application deadline is displayed on the programme page, interested applicants should avoid unnecessary delays if the application form remains open.

APPLY NOW

Why the MYCP Policy Lab Matters for Young Migrants

The MYCP Policy Lab is built around the principle that young people affected by migration should have opportunities to contribute to policies concerning their lives and futures.

Climate change, technological transformation and changing labour markets are increasingly interconnected. These changes can have significant consequences for migrants and displaced communities, particularly younger generations preparing to enter or already participating in the workforce.

Creating opportunities for young migrants to participate in these discussions can bring lived experience into policy conversations that might otherwise be dominated by institutional or technical perspectives.

The Policy Lab therefore combines capacity building with participation. Young people learn about policymaking while simultaneously developing recommendations that can feed into MYCP’s broader advocacy.

Conclusion

The MYCP Policy Lab on Climate, Migration, AI & the Future of Work provides an international online space for young people on the move to learn about policymaking, exchange perspectives with experts and peers, and contribute to policy recommendations concerning some of the most significant challenges affecting migration and employment.

Through expert sessions, thematic discussions, collaborative teamwork and policy brief development, participants can strengthen their understanding of the climate-labour-migration nexus while gaining practical exposure to international policy development.

The programme is particularly notable for welcoming young people without requiring previous policy experience and for placing lived experience at the centre of discussions concerning migrant youth.

Participants will also have the opportunity to receive a certificate, expand their international networks and develop a policy brief, with the winning submission published by MYCP and incorporated into its COP31 advocacy.

However, prospective applicants should carefully verify the programme dates before applying. The official MYCP webpage currently states that applications are open while displaying the Policy Lab dates as 10–11 October 2025, with final presentations scheduled for 17 or 18 October. No specific application deadline is currently published.

Interested young people should therefore consult the official MYCP Policy Lab webpage and application form for the latest programme information before submitting an application.

item.content:encoded:
NIH Graduate Partnerships Program (GPP) offers doctoral students interested in conducting advanced biomedical, behavioral, social science, and health-related research an extensive research training opportunity to undertake all or part of their dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.

The Graduate Partnerships Program connects doctoral education at universities in the United States and abroad with the research environment, facilities, scientists, and resources available across NIH Institutes and Centers. Through the program, participating students remain enrolled as full-time doctoral students at their universities while completing dissertation research under the guidance of NIH researchers.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to doctoral researchers working across fields such as biology, engineering, epidemiology, psychology, mathematics, chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, nursing, physics, computer science, bioinformatics, and other disciplines related to health and biomedical research.

Importantly, the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program provides financial support to participating students. Graduate student stipends are adjusted annually and based on relevant experience after completion of an undergraduate degree. Additional support includes health insurance coverage and, for eligible new fellows relocating near an NIH campus, a one-time relocation benefit of $1,500.

There are two primary routes into the Graduate Partnerships Program: Individual Partnerships and Institutional Partnerships. The appropriate pathway depends on a student’s university, current doctoral status, and the structure through which they plan to undertake their NIH dissertation research.

About the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is designed to give doctoral students an opportunity to perform dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program while continuing their academic studies through their home universities.

Students participating through institutional partnerships benefit from both the academic resources of their universities and the research environment of NIH. Under these arrangements, students complete their academic requirements through their universities while performing all or part of their dissertation research within an NIH research group.

Rather than replacing a student’s university doctoral programme, the NIH experience becomes an important component of it. Participants remain responsible for satisfying the academic requirements established by their home institution while simultaneously undertaking research at NIH.

This model can provide doctoral researchers with access to a broad scientific community while allowing them to maintain their existing academic affiliation.

Two Ways to Participate in the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Prospective participants should understand that the Graduate Partnerships Program offers two main pathways.

1. Individual Partnerships

Individual Partnerships are intended for students who are already enrolled in doctoral programmes at universities around the world.

Through this pathway, currently enrolled doctoral students may undertake all or part of their dissertation research at NIH.

Individual Partnerships can include:

  • U.S. citizens;
  • U.S. permanent residents; and
  • foreign nationals.

This makes the Individual Partnership pathway particularly significant for doctoral students studying outside the United States who are interested in conducting dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Individual Partnership applications are open year-round.

Students should review the specific Individual Partnership eligibility requirements and application process before submitting an application.

2. Institutional Partnerships

Institutional Partnerships are established collaborative arrangements between NIH and specific university programmes.

Students participating in these partnerships are jointly selected through NIH and university processes, complete their academic requirements at the relevant university, and undertake all or part of their dissertation research in an NIH Intramural Research Program research group.

The listed partner programmes include partnerships involving:

  • Brown University;
  • Georgetown University;
  • Johns Hopkins University;
  • University of Pennsylvania;
  • University College London;
  • University of Oxford and University of Cambridge; and
  • the Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program.

Applicants should note that eligibility requirements, university application requirements, programme structures, and deadlines can differ significantly between individual institutional partnerships.

What Degrees Are Eligible for the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program?

The broader NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is designed for doctoral-level students.

According to the NIH programme information provided, students pursuing the following degrees may participate:

  • PhD;
  • DPhil;
  • PharmD;
  • DrPH;
  • PsyD;
  • MD/PhD; and
  • DVM/PhD.

Students pursuing a master’s degree are not the intended participants for the Graduate Partnerships Program and are instead directed by NIH towards its Academic Internship Program.

The Graduate Partnerships Program is also not intended for students pursuing stand-alone professional degrees such as:

  • MD;
  • DO;
  • DDS; or
  • other professional degrees that do not fit the programme’s doctoral research structure.

Applicants should carefully review the requirements of the specific Individual or Institutional Partnership they intend to pursue, as individual pathways may have additional eligibility conditions.

Research Opportunities Available Through the NIH GPP

Graduate students participating in the programme undertake research within one of the NIH Institutes or Centers that form part of the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Research groups operate across NIH campuses, including the main NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

Graduate students work within research groups directed by NIH Principal Investigators (PIs).

The programme encompasses research opportunities across the:

  • biomedical sciences;
  • behavioral sciences;
  • social sciences;
  • basic sciences;
  • translational research; and
  • clinical research.

The institutional programme specifically invites graduate students interested in fields including biology, engineering, epidemiology, psychology, mathematics, chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, nursing, physics, computer science, bioinformatics, and other health-related disciplines.

This multidisciplinary structure means the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is not restricted solely to traditional laboratory-based biomedical research.

Fields of Study Relevant to the Programme

Students with academic or research experience across a wide variety of scientific and health-related disciplines may find relevant opportunities through the programme.

These include, but are not necessarily limited to:

  1. Biology
  2. Biomedical sciences
  3. Engineering
  4. Epidemiology
  5. Psychology
  6. Mathematics
  7. Chemistry
  8. Pharmaceutical sciences
  9. Nursing
  10. Physics
  11. Computer science
  12. Bioinformatics
  13. Behavioral sciences
  14. Social sciences
  15. Other health-related disciplines

Applicants should research the NIH Institutes and Centers carefully to identify research groups whose scientific focus aligns with their doctoral research interests and long-term academic or professional goals.

Where Will Graduate Students Conduct Their Research?

Graduate students can work within research groups across NIH campuses.

The programme is therefore not limited exclusively to one research building or scientific department. Students should research the different NIH campuses and understand the specific areas of work conducted at each location before pursuing a placement.

For Institutional Partnerships, these are full-time research positions within NIH Institutes and Centers, and participating students may work across NIH campuses, including the main campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

Students should also remember that their university remains an important part of their doctoral education.

Depending on the partnership, students may be required to divide their time between their university and NIH.

Professional Development Beyond Dissertation Research

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program extends beyond laboratory or research training.

Participating graduate students also gain access to professional and personal development resources intended to support their progress as researchers and future professionals.

NIH graduate students have access to:

  • professional development programmes focused on competencies needed for research and healthcare careers;
  • educational and career advising; and
  • a comprehensive well-being and resilience programme.

These resources can complement the student’s scientific training by helping them consider career pathways, strengthen professional competencies, and navigate the demands associated with doctoral research.

NIH Graduate Partnerships Program Stipend

One of the major features of the Graduate Partnerships Program is the financial support available to participating graduate researchers.

NIH graduate student stipends are adjusted annually and determined based on the amount of relevant experience accumulated after completion of an undergraduate degree.

Students participating in the broader GPP while conducting dissertation research at NIH are required to be paid according to the NIH graduate stipend structure, including where funding originates from a university or doctoral fellowship.

Because stipend levels depend on experience and are adjusted annually, prospective applicants should consult the current NIH stipend information rather than assuming that all GPP students receive an identical amount.

Health Insurance Support

In addition to the graduate stipend, NIH provides a stipend supplement designed to cover the full cost of health insurance offered through the Foundation for Advanced Education in the Sciences (FAES).

The insurance provision includes coverage for:

  • medical needs;
  • dental needs; and
  • vision needs.

Coverage is available for individuals and families.

Applicants should review the applicable NIH and FAES information to understand the specific terms of health insurance coverage.

$1,500 Relocation Benefit

New fellows who need to relocate to the vicinity of an NIH campus may qualify for a one-time relocation benefit of $1,500.

This support is particularly relevant to students who must move in order to begin their research training at an NIH location.

Applicants should review the applicable relocation conditions to determine whether they qualify.

Transportation and Travel Support

Free parking is available on each NIH campus.

Graduate students at some campuses may also qualify to participate in the Transhare Program, which provides another transportation-related option for eligible participants.

Students participating through institutional agreements additionally receive funding for travel between NIH and their university. However, the specific arrangements vary according to the partnership.

Prospective applicants should therefore review the details of their particular institutional partnership rather than assuming identical travel benefits across every programme.

Eligibility Requirements

There is no single set of detailed eligibility requirements that applies identically to every GPP pathway.

Eligibility requirements for Individual Partnerships and Institutional Partnerships differ.

For Institutional Partnerships specifically, NIH states that eligibility requirements vary according to the partnership. Applicants must therefore consult the individual programme information for the university partnership that interests them.

At the broader programme level, applicants should pay particular attention to their:

  • doctoral enrolment status;
  • degree type;
  • academic discipline;
  • research interests;
  • university;
  • citizenship or immigration circumstances where applicable;
  • requirements of the particular partnership; and
  • ability to fulfil NIH onboarding requirements.

Federal Background Check Requirement

Regardless of the pathway through which a graduate student enters NIH, participants must be able to pass the required federal background check.

Applicants should take this requirement seriously and review NIH’s full terms and conditions before committing to the programme.

Meeting academic or research requirements alone does not remove the requirement to satisfy applicable NIH onboarding and federal requirements.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Participating in the Graduate Partnerships Program involves significant responsibilities.

A GPP participant remains a full-time student at their university while undertaking dissertation research through NIH.

For Institutional Partnerships, the student is simultaneously a full-time university student and a trainee working onsite at an NIH campus. Institutional partnerships require students to spend time at their university, and some arrangements require the establishment of collaboration between an NIH Principal Investigator and a university Principal Investigator.

Students must continue meeting the academic requirements of their graduate programme while conducting their dissertation research at NIH.

Prospective applicants should therefore carefully investigate:

  1. How much time they will spend at NIH.
  2. How much time they will need to spend at their university.
  3. Their university’s doctoral requirements.
  4. NIH research expectations.
  5. The requirements of their specific partnership.
  6. Whether collaboration between university and NIH investigators is required.
  7. The research group and Principal Investigator they may work with.
  8. Funding, relocation, travel, and other practical considerations.

Understanding these requirements before applying can help students determine whether the structure is compatible with their doctoral programme.

NIH Graduate Partnerships Program 2026 Application Deadline

Deadlines depend on whether an applicant is pursuing an Individual Partnership or an Institutional Partnership.

Individual Partnerships

Applications are open year-round.

This means there is no single annual closing date for the Individual Partnership pathway based on the programme information provided.

Institutional Partnerships

The 2026 Institutional Partnership application is currently open.

The main applicant deadline is:

Tuesday, December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon Eastern Time.

The general deadline for references to submit recommendation letters is:

Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 12:00 noon Eastern Time.

However, NIH lists exceptions for certain institutional partnerships:

  • University of Pennsylvania: Tuesday, December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.
  • Johns Hopkins University: Friday, December 4, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.

NIH also notes that the Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program (CBSTP) operates two submission rounds, and prospective applicants should consult the CBSTP programme directly for its applicable deadline.

Because deadlines and requirements vary, applicants should verify the schedule for their selected partnership well before beginning the application.

How to Apply for the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Applicants should first determine whether they are applying through an Individual Partnership or Institutional Partnership.

They should then carefully review the eligibility and admission requirements associated with that pathway.

Applying for an Institutional Partnership

Applicants pursuing an Institutional Partnership must complete the NIH GPP application.

University application requirements can differ depending on the selected partnership.

The NIH online application includes several important components.

1. Undergraduate Experience

Applicants must provide information about their undergraduate educational experience.

2. Coursework and Grades

Applicants must provide a list of their coursework and grades.

Candidates should ensure that the academic information entered into the application is complete and accurate.

3. Curriculum Vitae

A current CV must be included.

Applicants should ensure that their CV clearly communicates relevant academic, research, technical, professional, and other experiences appropriate to the programme.

4. Personal Statement

Applicants must submit a personal statement.

According to the NIH application requirements, the statement should address:

  • previous research experiences;
  • why the applicant is interested in the particular institutional agreement;
  • long-term career goals; and
  • barriers experienced during the applicant’s educational journey.

The personal statement therefore provides applicants with an opportunity to explain both their scientific preparation and their motivation for pursuing the specific NIH-university partnership.

5. Three References

Applicants must provide the names and contact information of three references.

Applicants should pay close attention to recommendation deadlines, particularly because references generally have a separate deadline from the applicant.

6. Complete the Partner University’s Application Where Required

Submitting the NIH application may not be the only requirement.

Applicants may also need to submit a separate application to the relevant partner university.

The exact requirements differ between institutional partnerships, making it essential to review the programme-specific instructions before applying.

Institutional Partner Programmes

The NIH information provided identifies several established Institutional Partnership programmes.

They include:

  • Brown University Graduate Partnership Program
  • Georgetown University Graduate Partnership Program
  • Johns Hopkins University Graduate Partnership Program
  • University of Pennsylvania Graduate Partnership Program
  • University College London PhD – England
  • University of Oxford-Cambridge PhD – England
  • University of Oxford/Cambridge MD/PhD – Track 1 and Track 2, England
  • Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program (CBSTP)

Each partnership should be treated as a distinct opportunity within the broader GPP structure because eligibility, academic arrangements, university requirements, and deadlines may vary.

Why Applicants Should Research NIH Institutes and Centers Before Applying

A strong application should be informed by an understanding of the NIH research environment.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to investigate the NIH Intramural Research Program, individual NIH Institutes and Centers, NIH campuses, and the specific research conducted at those locations.

This is especially important because doctoral students work within research groups led by Principal Investigators.

Applicants should consider how their dissertation interests connect with:

  • a particular NIH Institute or Center;
  • an NIH research group;
  • the work of relevant Principal Investigators;
  • their university research programme; and
  • their long-term scientific and professional goals.

This preparation can also help applicants explain why a particular partnership or research environment is appropriate for their doctoral development.

Key Benefits of the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Depending on the applicable partnership and individual circumstances, major features of the programme include:

  • The opportunity to undertake all or part of doctoral dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.
  • Access to research groups across NIH Institutes and Centers.
  • Research training under NIH Principal Investigators.
  • Opportunities spanning biomedical, behavioral, social, basic, translational, and clinical research.
  • NIH graduate student stipend support.
  • Annual stipend adjustments based on post-undergraduate experience.
  • A stipend supplement covering eligible FAES health insurance costs.
  • Medical, dental, and vision coverage through the applicable insurance arrangement.
  • A one-time $1,500 relocation benefit for eligible new fellows moving near an NIH campus.
  • Free parking at NIH campuses.
  • Potential access to Transhare at eligible campuses.
  • Travel support between NIH and the university for students participating in institutional agreements, subject to partnership-specific arrangements.
  • Professional development programmes.
  • Educational and career advising.
  • Well-being and resilience resources.
  • The opportunity to combine university-based doctoral education with research experience in the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should consider completing the following steps:

  1. Determine whether the Individual or Institutional Partnership route applies to you.
  2. Confirm that your doctoral degree is compatible with the GPP.
  3. Review the specific eligibility requirements for your chosen pathway.
  4. Research the NIH Intramural Research Program.
  5. Explore relevant NIH Institutes and Centers.
  6. Investigate NIH campuses and research areas.
  7. Review the requirements of the relevant university partnership, where applicable.
  8. Prepare information about your undergraduate experience.
  9. Compile your coursework and grades.
  10. Update your CV.
  11. Prepare your personal statement if applying through the relevant institutional route.
  12. Identify three appropriate references.
  13. Confirm recommendation letter deadlines.
  14. Determine whether a separate university application is required.
  15. Review federal background check requirements.
  16. Verify the deadline applicable to your particular partnership.
  17. Submit all required materials through the appropriate NIH application system.

APPLY NOW

Important Deadline Summary

Applicants should not assume that every Graduate Partnerships Program pathway follows the same application calendar.

For the current cycle described by NIH:

Individual Partnerships: Applications are open year-round.

Institutional Partnerships: Applications are open, with the main applicant deadline of December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.

General recommendation letter deadline: December 3, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET, with partnership-specific exceptions.

Prospective applicants should confirm the requirements of their chosen programme before submission because certain institutional partnerships operate under different deadlines and procedures.

Contact for Questions

Applicants with questions about the Graduate Partnerships Program can consult the NIH Office of Intramural Training & Education’s frequently asked questions or contact the programme directly at:

Email: gpp@nih.gov

Applicants are strongly encouraged to use official NIH information when checking eligibility requirements, deadlines, programme structures, and application procedures.

Conclusion

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program 2026 offers doctoral researchers an opportunity to integrate university-based graduate education with dissertation research in the National Institutes of Health Intramural Research Program.

Through Individual and Institutional Partnerships, students can undertake research across biomedical, behavioral, social, computational, engineering, pharmaceutical, and other health-related fields while working within NIH research groups led by Principal Investigators.

The programme also provides substantial support for participating graduate researchers. Depending on eligibility and partnership arrangements, this can include an NIH graduate stipend, health insurance support covering medical, dental and vision needs, a $1,500 relocation benefit for eligible new fellows, transportation provisions, professional development, career advising, and additional support resources.

For prospective applicants, choosing the correct pathway is essential. Individual Partnership applications remain open throughout the year, while the current Institutional Partnership cycle has a principal applicant deadline of December 1, 2026 at noon ET, with recommendation letters and certain partner programmes following separate deadlines.

Doctoral students interested in the programme should carefully examine the relevant partnership, research NIH Institutes and Centers that align with their interests, prepare the required academic and application materials, and verify all programme-specific requirements before submitting an application.
