item.content:encoded:
The WHO/IBP Network has launched a new funding opportunity for community-based organizations working to transform sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and rights through locally driven action.

The SPARK Grant Program — Shifting Power through Action and Reciprocal Knowledge Exchange — will provide between 5 and 10 grants of up to USD 20,000 each to youth-led, women-led and Indigenous-led community-based organizations. Selected projects will run for approximately one year and should demonstrate how communities can adapt, apply and improve the use of World Health Organization guidelines, tools and evidence in real-world settings.

Unlike funding calls that ask community organizations simply to implement externally designed programmes, SPARK is deliberately framed around community leadership, power shifting and reciprocal learning. The WHO/IBP Network wants applicants to demonstrate how communities themselves are influencing priorities, making decisions, adapting evidence and determining what effective sexual, reproductive and broader maternal and child health programming looks like in their own contexts.

The programme is particularly interested in approaches that connect sexual and reproductive health and rights with areas such as maternal health, climate, livelihoods and poverty reduction, education and faith-based initiatives.

Organizations from across the world may be considered. The programme states that it aims to support at least one organization from each of the six WHO regions: the African Region, Region of the Americas, South-East Asia Region, European Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region and Western Pacific Region.

Applications can be submitted in English, French or Spanish.

Application deadline: 9 October 2026

Grant amount: Up to USD 20,000 per organization

Number of anticipated grants: 5–10

Implementation period: One year

Apply here: SPARK Grant Application Form

About the WHO/IBP Network SPARK Grant Program

SPARK stands for:

Shifting Power through Action and Reciprocal Knowledge Exchange.

The programme has been developed by the WHO/IBP Network to place communities more directly at the centre of sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and rights work.

Its central premise is that effective implementation of global health guidance should not operate only from the top down.

WHO develops guidelines, tools and evidence-based products, but their usefulness ultimately depends on how they are:

  • Understood
  • Adapted
  • Applied
  • Interpreted
  • Improved
  • Shared

within actual communities.

SPARK therefore seeks organizations that are already thinking critically about how international evidence can be translated into local action.

The programme asks community organizations not simply to demonstrate that they have used WHO materials, but to show how they are reshaping the use of those materials around community priorities, lived experience and local knowledge.

What Is the Main Purpose of SPARK?

The programme has several closely related objectives.

First, it seeks to support community-led implementation of WHO sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health guidance.

Second, it aims to strengthen approaches in which communities participate meaningfully in:

  • Programme design
  • Decision-making
  • Implementation
  • Monitoring
  • Evaluation
  • Learning

Third, it seeks to identify innovative local practices that can be shared across the wider IBP Network.

Fourth, SPARK is intended to generate learning that may help the WHO/IBP Network understand:

  • How WHO guidance is being used in practice
  • How local organizations adapt formal global guidance
  • What implementation barriers remain
  • Where evidence or guidance gaps exist
  • How community leadership can improve programme relevance

The programme is therefore both a funding mechanism and a learning initiative.

SPARK Is About Shifting Power, Not Only Delivering Services

One of the most important elements of the call is its emphasis on power shifting.

Applicants are expected to go beyond describing community participation as outreach or consultation.

The programme wants to know how communities influence actual decisions.

For example, an organization might demonstrate that community members:

  • Decide which health issues should be prioritized
  • Help design interventions
  • Determine culturally appropriate implementation approaches
  • Participate in budget or activity decisions
  • Define what success should look like
  • Lead monitoring and evaluation
  • Help interpret project results
  • Determine how learning should be shared

The distinction is important.

SPARK is not merely asking whether communities are involved in delivering an organization’s programme.

It is asking whether communities are meaningfully shaping the programme itself.

Who Should Apply?

The programme strongly encourages applications from organizations that are:

  • Youth-led
  • Women-led
  • Indigenous-led
  • Community-based
  • Working directly with the populations they serve

Applicants should also generally have been operating for at least:

Two years

and should have previous implementation experience using at least:

One WHO guideline, tool or product.

Organizations should therefore be able to demonstrate both community leadership and some practical familiarity with WHO evidence or implementation resources.

Priority for Organizations New to WHO and IBP Funding

The SPARK programme specifically states that priority will be given to organizations that are:

  • New to WHO funding mechanisms
  • New to IBP Network funding mechanisms
  • Strongly accountable to their communities
  • Demonstrably community-led

This could make the call especially important for smaller or locally rooted organizations that may have strong implementation experience but limited previous access to major international funding systems.

Being new to WHO or IBP funding is not described as an absolute eligibility requirement.

It is a priority factor.

Organizations with previous relationships with WHO or IBP are therefore not explicitly excluded, but organizations with limited previous access may receive particular consideration.

What Types of Projects Is SPARK Looking For?

The programme is interested in organizations applying WHO guidelines and tools in ways that are:

  • Innovative
  • Locally grounded
  • Community-led
  • Responsive to real implementation challenges
  • Capable of generating useful learning

Applicants should clearly explain how their project uses or adapts relevant WHO guidance.

This might involve a formal WHO guideline, implementation tool, technical product or another relevant WHO resource connected with sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child or adolescent health.

Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights

Projects may focus directly on sexual and reproductive health and rights.

Relevant areas may include issues such as:

  • Family planning
  • Contraception
  • Adolescent sexual and reproductive health
  • Maternal health
  • Reproductive health information
  • Gender-responsive services
  • Community engagement
  • Access to evidence-based care

However, SPARK is especially interested in work that connects health programming with issues outside conventional health-sector boundaries.

Priority Intersection: Maternal Health

Maternal health is explicitly highlighted as one of the programme’s priority intersections.

Projects might explore how community-led implementation of WHO guidance can strengthen areas such as:

  • Maternal health information
  • Quality of care
  • Community referral systems
  • Birth preparedness
  • Respectful care
  • Community accountability
  • Access to appropriate services

Applicants should still connect the project to relevant WHO guidance or tools.

Priority Intersection: Climate

SPARK is also interested in projects at the intersection of sexual and reproductive health and climate-related challenges.

Climate change can affect health through mechanisms such as:

  • Displacement
  • Drought
  • Flooding
  • Food insecurity
  • Migration
  • Health-system disruption
  • Livelihood loss

Community-led organizations may be especially well positioned to explain how these pressures affect sexual, reproductive and maternal health differently across populations.

The programme provides space for organizations to develop solutions grounded in local realities rather than treating health and climate as separate policy areas.

Priority Intersection: Workforce, Livelihoods and Poverty Reduction

The programme also welcomes proposals integrating health with:

  • Employment
  • Livelihoods
  • Workforce issues
  • Economic security
  • Poverty reduction

This recognizes that health outcomes are affected by economic circumstances.

For example, access to sexual and reproductive healthcare may be influenced by:

  • Income
  • Employment insecurity
  • Transport costs
  • Care responsibilities
  • Workplace policies
  • Economic dependence

Projects can therefore examine how WHO guidance might be implemented more effectively when economic and livelihood realities are considered.

Priority Intersection: Education

Education is another highlighted area.

Applicants might examine how sexual, reproductive, maternal or adolescent health work can be integrated with:

  • Schools
  • Universities
  • Community education
  • Youth learning spaces
  • Informal education systems

Youth-led organizations may be particularly well placed to develop innovative models that connect evidence-based health guidance with education environments.

Priority Intersection: Faith-Based Initiatives

Faith is also explicitly included among the programme’s areas of interest.

Faith-based organizations and community actors can have substantial influence over:

  • Social norms
  • Community trust
  • Health beliefs
  • Family decision-making
  • Gender expectations
  • Health-seeking behaviour

SPARK therefore welcomes approaches that engage faith settings while remaining grounded in evidence-based WHO guidance and community leadership.

Other Areas May Also Be Considered

The programme’s list of intersections is not presented as completely exhaustive.

The concept-note requirements allow applicants to identify:

  • Health
  • Maternal health
  • Climate
  • Workforce
  • Education
  • Faith
  • Other relevant sectors

Organizations with strong proposals outside the examples listed may therefore still be able to demonstrate alignment if their project is clearly connected with the programme’s overall objectives.

What Does SPARK Mean by Reciprocal Knowledge Exchange?

The phrase “reciprocal knowledge exchange” is central to the programme.

Traditional technical-assistance models sometimes assume that knowledge moves in one direction:

From international institutions to local organizations.

SPARK emphasizes a different relationship.

WHO guidance and evidence can inform community programmes, but community implementation also produces valuable knowledge that can inform institutions.

The flow of learning therefore works in both directions.

A community organization might learn from WHO evidence while simultaneously helping WHO and the IBP Network understand:

  • Which recommendations are practical
  • Which recommendations need adaptation
  • What communities perceive differently
  • Which implementation barriers are overlooked
  • Which innovations are emerging locally
  • Where global guidance remains incomplete

That reciprocal process is one of the programme’s most distinctive features.

Grant Amount

Selected organizations may receive up to:

USD 20,000 per grant.

Applicants may propose a budget below that amount where appropriate.

The concept note must include a proposed budget explaining how the requested funding would support the planned work.

The call does not state that every selected organization will automatically receive exactly USD 20,000.

The correct description is therefore:

Up to USD 20,000 per grant.

Number of Grants

The WHO/IBP Network anticipates awarding approximately:

5 to 10 grants.

Because the programme aims to support at least one organization from every WHO region, the final portfolio is expected to have broad geographic representation.

However, the call describes this regional distribution as an aim, rather than an absolute guarantee that a grant will be made in every region regardless of application quality.

Duration

Projects are expected to run for:

One year.

Applicants should therefore propose activities and milestones that can realistically be completed during a 12-month implementation period.

Geographic Reach

The programme has a global scope.

The WHO/IBP Network aims to fund organizations across all six WHO regions:

  1. African Region
  2. Region of the Americas
  3. South-East Asia Region
  4. European Region
  5. Eastern Mediterranean Region
  6. Western Pacific Region

This means the opportunity is not limited to Africa, Asia or any single group of developing countries.

Eligible organizations may potentially come from countries throughout the world, provided they satisfy the substantive requirements of the call.

What Will Selected Organizations Receive?

The SPARK programme offers more than grant funding.

Successful grantees are expected to receive a combination of:

  • Flexible financial support
  • Technical assistance
  • Peer learning
  • Global networking
  • Visibility opportunities

Direct and Flexible Funding

Selected organizations will receive direct grant funding to implement their approved activities.

The call specifically describes the funding as:

Flexible grant funding.

This is particularly relevant for community-based organizations because rigid funding structures can make it difficult to adapt implementation to changing local circumstances.

Technical Support From WHO and the IBP Network

Grantees will receive technical support from the:

WHO/IBP Network

and access to relevant WHO sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health guidelines and tools.

This means organizations can receive technical engagement alongside financial support.

Access to Global Communities of Practice

SPARK grantees will also connect to the IBP Network’s global Communities of Practice.

The call identifies several networks, including:

  • WHO Guidelines Community of Practice
  • Adolescent Community of Practice
  • Women’s Health Community of Practice
  • Powershifting Community of Practice

These networks can allow organizations to:

  • Share experiences
  • Learn from peers
  • Discuss implementation challenges
  • Exchange adaptations
  • Build relationships across countries and regions

Opportunities to Showcase Community Work

Grantees may also have opportunities to document and present their work to a global audience working on sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health.

This visibility can help organizations share:

  • Implementation lessons
  • Community innovations
  • Challenges
  • Adaptations
  • Evidence gaps
  • Approaches to shifting power

The programme therefore places significant emphasis on documentation and learning.

Initial Application: 500-Word Concept Note

The first stage of the application is deliberately concise.

Applicants must submit a:

Concept note of no more than 500 words.

This means organizations need to communicate their proposal clearly and efficiently.

The concept note should contain six major elements.

1. Organizational Overview

Applicants should explain:

  • Who the organization is
  • How long it has operated
  • Which communities it serves
  • Its implementation experience
  • Its experience using WHO guidelines or tools
  • Its leadership structure

The leadership structure should clearly demonstrate whether the organization is:

  • Youth-led
  • Women-led
  • Indigenous-led

or falls within more than one of these categories.

2. Proposed Activity

Applicants should explain what they intend to do.

The description should identify:

  • Main activities
  • Target community
  • Problem being addressed
  • WHO guideline, tool or product being used
  • How the WHO resource will be applied or adapted
  • Relevant sector of integration

The proposal should therefore connect the project directly to concrete WHO resources rather than referring vaguely to global health guidance.

3. Power-Shifting Approach

Applicants need to explain how community members will influence the project.

This section should address:

  • Community leadership
  • Decision-making
  • Programme design
  • Accountability
  • Evaluation
  • Ownership

Applicants should avoid describing community members only as beneficiaries.

The call clearly values proposals where communities exercise meaningful influence.

4. Budget

Applicants should provide a proposed budget of:

Up to USD 20,000.

Even at the concept-note stage, the budget should logically correspond with the proposed activities.

Applicants should make sure the requested amount is proportionate to:

  • Project scale
  • Implementation period
  • Activities
  • Staffing needs
  • Community participation
  • Documentation requirements

5. Implementation Timeline

Applicants should provide a timeline identifying:

  • Major activities
  • Key milestones
  • Implementation sequence

The full project should fit within the programme’s one-year duration.

6. Documentation and Learning Plan

This section is particularly important because SPARK emphasizes reciprocal knowledge exchange.

Applicants should explain how they will:

  • Record implementation experience
  • Capture community learning
  • Identify challenges
  • Document adaptations
  • Share findings locally
  • Share findings with the IBP Network

The documentation process should ideally be useful both to the community and to wider global health practitioners.

What Happens After the Concept Note?

The initial 500-word submission is only the first stage.

Shortlisted applicants may be invited to submit a more formal proposal.

That later stage may require additional documentation, including:

  • Financial statements
  • One letter of support
  • Information required under WHO procedures for engagement with non-state actors

Organizations should therefore make sure their institutional documentation is reasonably organized before applying.

Application Languages

Applications may be submitted in:

  • English
  • French
  • Spanish

This broadens accessibility for organizations across multiple WHO regions.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the official online application form.

Application form:
Submit a SPARK Grant Concept Note

Before starting, organizations should prepare:

  1. A concise organizational description.
  2. Evidence of at least two years of operation.
  3. Details showing youth, women and/or Indigenous leadership.
  4. Evidence of previous use of a WHO guideline, tool or product.
  5. A clearly defined project idea.
  6. The relevant WHO resource to be used or adapted.
  7. A power-shifting approach.
  8. A budget of no more than USD 20,000.
  9. A one-year implementation plan.
  10. A documentation and learning approach.

Application Deadline

The final deadline is:

9 October 2026

Organizations should submit before the deadline and allow sufficient time for internal review of the 500-word concept note.

Questions about the programme can be directed to:

ibpnetwork@who.int

How to Develop a Strong SPARK Concept Note

Because applicants have only 500 words, clarity will matter considerably.

Make Community Leadership Visible

Do not simply state:

“Our organization works with young people.”

Explain who leads.

For example:

  • What proportion of leadership roles are held by young people?
  • Who makes strategic decisions?
  • How does the target community influence priorities?
  • How is accountability maintained?

Name the WHO Guidance You Use

The programme asks specifically for applicants with previous experience implementing at least one WHO guideline, tool or product.

A stronger proposal should clearly identify:

  • The exact WHO resource
  • How the organization previously used it
  • How it will be used or adapted under SPARK

Avoid vague statements such as:

“We follow WHO guidance.”

Explain the Innovation

Innovation does not necessarily require new technology.

Innovation might mean:

  • Applying WHO guidance in a new setting
  • Integrating health and livelihoods
  • Connecting reproductive health and climate adaptation
  • Working through faith networks
  • Giving adolescents formal decision-making authority
  • Adapting guidance through Indigenous knowledge systems
  • Developing new community accountability mechanisms

Explain what is different and why it matters.

Demonstrate Real Power Shifting

This is one of the most important elements of the call.

Applicants should explain how the community moves from being:

Recipient → participant → decision-maker.

A strong proposal will show who has authority and how that authority operates in practice.

Keep the Project Realistic

The maximum award is USD 20,000 and the project period is one year.

The strongest proposals are likely to present focused, achievable work rather than overly ambitious national programmes requiring far greater resources.

Include Learning, Not Only Activities

SPARK specifically wants knowledge that can benefit other organizations and inform how WHO guidance is implemented.

Applicants should therefore think about:

  • What will you learn?
  • How will you know?
  • Who will document it?
  • How will the community use the findings?
  • How will the IBP Network learn from it?

Key Information at a Glance

Programme: SPARK — Shifting Power through Action and Reciprocal Knowledge Exchange

Organizer: WHO/IBP Network

Published: 17 September 2026

Primary focus: Community-led sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and rights

Target organizations: Youth-led, women-led and Indigenous-led community-based organizations

Minimum operating history: At least two years

WHO experience: Previous implementation experience using at least one WHO guideline, tool or product

Grant amount: Up to USD 20,000

Number of grants: 5–10

Duration: One year

Geographic scope: Global, across all six WHO regions

Priority sectors: Maternal health, climate, livelihoods/poverty reduction, education, faith-based initiatives and related areas

Application stage: Initial concept note of no more than 500 words

Application languages: English, French or Spanish

Deadline: 9 October 2026

Application: Official SPARK Application Form

Contact: ibpnetwork@who.int

Conclusion

The WHO/IBP Network SPARK Grant Program 2026 offers a distinctive funding opportunity for community-based organizations seeking to strengthen sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health through locally led implementation.

With 5–10 grants of up to USD 20,000 each, the programme is intentionally focused on organizations led by the communities most directly affected by health policies and programmes, particularly youth-led, women-led and Indigenous-led organizations.

SPARK’s central emphasis is not simply service delivery. It is about changing who holds influence over programme design and implementation.

Applicants are expected to demonstrate how they use WHO evidence while also generating knowledge that can travel back into global health systems. Communities are therefore positioned not merely as recipients of WHO guidance, but as sources of expertise whose experiences can improve how guidance is interpreted and used.

The programme is especially interested in projects linking sexual and reproductive health and rights with maternal health, climate, livelihoods, poverty reduction, education and faith-based action.

Successful organizations will receive not only flexible funding, but also technical support, access to IBP Communities of Practice and opportunities to share their work with global sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health audiences.

Organizations should begin by developing a focused 500-word concept note covering their organizational background, proposed activities, relevant WHO guidance, approach to shifting power, budget, timeline and learning plan.

Applications close on 9 October 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Visa has opened applications for a new wave of 2027 internships, new college graduate roles and rotational development programmes, creating opportunities for university students and recent graduates interested in building careers across technology, product management, sales, consulting, analytics, marketing and business leadership.

The newest U.S. 2027 recruitment cycle includes paid internships in software engineering, product management and sales, alongside full-time rotational programmes for new graduates. Visa’s Early Careers portal is also currently displaying internship opportunities in Europe, Africa, Central Asia and other markets, although deadlines and work-authorization requirements vary by individual vacancy.

For several of the newly launched U.S. roles, Visa explicitly states that applications are being accepted from 17 September through 24 September 2026, while the Workday system displays an end date of 25 September 2026 on some individual postings. Applicants should therefore treat 24 September 2026 as the safest deadline for the newly launched U.S. 2027 cycle and apply as early as possible.

Official Visa Early Careers portal

About Visa’s Early Careers Programmes

Visa operates one of the world’s largest electronic payments networks and recruits students and graduates into early-career positions across its technology and commercial businesses.

The company’s current early-career openings span several career pathways, including:

  • Software engineering and technology
  • Product management
  • Sales and business development
  • Visa Consulting & Analytics
  • Marketing
  • Client services
  • Data, analytics and artificial intelligence
  • Strategy and operations
  • Value-Added Services
  • Leadership development

The structure varies by programme and country. Some positions are conventional summer internships lasting around 11 or 12 weeks, while others are semester internships, cooperative placements or full-time graduate programmes.

Visa’s U.S. internship programme, for example, is described as a 12-week immersive experience in which students work on substantive projects, participate in professional-development sessions and conclude the programme by presenting their work to Visa leaders.

Newly Open Visa 2027 Internships in the United States

The most recent 2027 U.S. recruitment launch includes several substantial internship opportunities.

1. Associate Product Manager Intern – Summer 2027

Location: Foster City, California
Job ID: REF088603W
Field: Product Management
Work arrangement: Hybrid
Estimated pay: USD 46–55 per hour
Graduation window: December 2027–August 2028

Visa’s Associate Product Manager internship gives students exposure to the full product lifecycle, from understanding customer problems and researching markets to roadmapping, product development, testing and commercialization.

Interns may work across:

  • Product strategy and discovery
  • Customer problem definition
  • Business cases
  • Product roadmaps
  • Requirements documentation
  • Market and user research
  • Design and engineering collaboration
  • Product launches
  • Go-to-market strategy

The programme is particularly notable because strong interns may be considered for Visa’s two-year Associate Product Manager full-time rotational programme after graduation. That programme includes four six-month rotations intended to develop future product leaders.

Applicants should be pursuing a bachelor’s or master’s degree, with the role particularly relevant to students in areas such as business administration, management information systems, operations, communications, design, product management, computer science, engineering, data science, mathematics or statistics.

Visa states that it will not provide current or future work-visa sponsorship for this U.S. role.

View the Associate Product Manager Intern vacancy

2. Sales Development Program Intern – Summer 2027

Location: Atlanta, Georgia
Job ID: REF088567W
Field: Sales and Business Development
Estimated pay: USD 29–33 per hour
Graduation window: December 2027–August 2028

This internship is designed for students interested in careers at the intersection of technology, payments, sales and client engagement.

Interns can expect to support work involving:

  • Client and market research
  • Pipeline development
  • Sales analytics
  • CRM tools
  • Business insights
  • Cross-functional collaboration
  • Presentations
  • Client engagement

No previous professional sales experience is expressly required. Visa instead emphasizes interest in technology, financial services and client work, along with communication, analytical ability and willingness to learn.

Students studying areas such as sales, business administration, economics, data analytics, international business, management information systems and related subjects may be particularly well aligned.

A strong internship performance may lead to consideration for Visa’s two-and-a-half-year Sales Development Program, which provides rotational exposure and structured professional development after graduation.

Visa does not offer work-visa sponsorship for this U.S. internship.

View the Sales Development Program Internship

3. Software Engineer Intern – Bellevue, Washington – 2027

Location: Bellevue, Washington
Job ID: REF088585W
Field: Software Engineering
Programme duration: Approximately 12 weeks
Estimated pay: USD 41–48 per hour
Graduation window: December 2027–August 2028

The Bellevue internship places students within Visa’s technology teams to work on real engineering projects.

Examples provided by Visa include:

  • Deploying Kafka clusters with Docker and Kubernetes
  • Developing natural-language chatbots
  • Automating payment processes
  • Creating testing and monitoring tools
  • Building solutions for digital-currency transaction routing
  • Developing mobile-banking application frameworks
  • Working across the software-development lifecycle

Visa seeks students pursuing degrees such as:

  • Computer Science
  • Computer Engineering
  • CIS/MIS
  • Cybersecurity
  • Business with relevant technical preparation
  • Related disciplines

Preferred technical experience may include languages and tools such as Java, C/C++, C#, .NET, Python, JavaScript, HTML, REST and Selenium.

Visa states that work-visa sponsorship and future sponsorship are not available for this position.

View the Bellevue Software Engineer Internship

4. Software Engineer Intern – Austin, Texas – 2027

Location: Austin, Texas
Job ID: REF088544W
Field: Software Engineering
Estimated pay: USD 39–46 per hour
Graduation window: December 2027–August 2028

The Austin Software Engineer internship follows the same broader 12-week Visa internship structure while placing students in technology teams in Austin.

Possible projects include software development, testing, automation, payment systems, cloud or platform-related work and digital-payment infrastructure.

Applicants are expected to be pursuing a bachelor’s or master’s degree in areas such as:

  • Computer Science
  • Computer Engineering
  • CIS/MIS
  • Cybersecurity
  • Business
  • Related technical disciplines

Visa again states that it will not sponsor work visas in connection with this role, including future sponsorship.

View the Austin Software Engineer Internship

5. Visa 2027 Sophomore Internship Program – Software Engineer Intern

Location: Bellevue, Washington
Job ID: REF088594W
Field: Software Engineering
Estimated pay: USD 41–48 per hour
Graduation window: December 2028–August 2029

Visa also has a separate Sophomore Internship Program, intended for students at an earlier stage of university.

The programme offers a 12-week experience combining:

  • Technical project work
  • Mentorship
  • Professional-development workshops
  • Networking
  • Business and communication skills
  • Exposure to future internship pathways

The programme is designed partly as an early talent pipeline, with the possibility for strong participants to continue toward future Visa internship opportunities and eventually full-time careers.

Applicants should generally be pursuing a relevant bachelor’s or master’s degree and expect to graduate between December 2028 and August 2029.

Visa does not provide work-visa sponsorship for this role.

View the 2027 Sophomore Software Engineering Internship

Other Internship Opportunities Currently Showing Open on Visa’s Early Careers Portal

Visa’s live Early Careers portal is international, so the U.S. roles above are not the only internship opportunities presently visible.

The following roles were also showing an active Apply option when checked.

Opportunity Location Main Area Key Applicant Profile
Marketing Intern – Students Graduating Summer 2028 or December 2027 Casablanca, Morocco Marketing Bachelor’s/Master’s students in marketing, business, communications, economics, finance or related fields
VAS Intern – Students Graduating Summer 2028 or December 2027 Casablanca, Morocco Value-Added Services / Business Analysis Students in business, finance, economics, marketing, analytics, engineering or information systems
VCA Intern – Morocco Casablanca, Morocco Consulting & Analytics Bachelor’s/Master’s students; business, economics, finance, engineering, mathematics, analytics and related fields encouraged
Issuing VAS Intern Baku, Azerbaijan Sales / Value-Added Services Students graduating Dec. 2027–Summer 2028 in business, marketing, finance, economics, analytics, engineering or related areas
VCA Intern Almaty, Kazakhstan Consulting & Analytics Students in economics, business, finance, econometrics, IT/MIS, engineering and related disciplines
Client Services Intern Almaty, Kazakhstan Client Services / Operations Students interested in payments, client management, operations and financial services
Marketing Services Intern Kyiv, Ukraine Marketing / Client Marketing Bachelor’s/Master’s students graduating Dec. 2027–Summer 2028
Data Solutions Strategy & Operations Intern Warsaw, Poland Strategy, Data and AI Students in business, economics, engineering, data, computer science or related fields
Software Engineer Intern Warsaw, Poland Technology Bachelor’s/Master’s students with programming ability and software-engineering interest
Consulting & Analytics Intern – Dutch Speaking Amsterdam, Netherlands Consulting Penultimate-year students completing university in 2027; English and Dutch required; permanent Netherlands work authorization required

Because the Visa portal changes continuously, vacancies can be added, amended or removed. Applicants should therefore use the main Early Careers page as the final authority immediately before applying.

Important Note About Older or Inconsistent Listings

A few Visa Early Careers vacancies currently remain searchable with an active “Apply” status even though some of the text references internship dates in 2026.

For example, the Almaty VCA internship currently states a graduation window extending into 2027–2028 but also refers to availability for a June–August 2026 internship.

The portal also currently surfaces a Consulting Intern – COOP Program in Cairo, but the text similarly refers to a June–August 2026 placement.

Applicants should therefore read the individual live vacancy carefully before submitting rather than assuming that every role appearing under Early Careers belongs to the same 2027 recruitment cycle.

Visa’s International Summer Internship Structure

Outside the United States, Visa describes many of its summer programmes as approximately 11 weeks long.

For example, Visa’s European Consulting & Analytics internship explains that interns participate in a global programme with development sessions, mentorship, exposure to client work and the possibility of progression into a graduate programme based on performance and business needs.

This demonstrates that Visa’s early-career recruitment model is often intended as a pipeline rather than a standalone short-term experience.

Strong interns may gain:

  • Practical work experience
  • Mentorship
  • Exposure to Visa leaders
  • Technical or commercial training
  • International payments-industry knowledge
  • Networking
  • Potential consideration for graduate employment

The exact progression model varies by country and programme.

Newly Open New College Graduate and Rotational Programmes

Visa’s September 2026 recruitment launch also includes several full-time graduate opportunities. These should not be confused with internships.

Associate Product Manager New College Graduate Rotational Program 2027

Based in the San Francisco Bay Area, this two-year programme consists of four six-month rotations across areas such as product strategy, development, commercialization, customer solutions, innovation, analytics and go-to-market work.

Applicants should generally have a bachelor’s or master’s degree graduating between May 2026 and August 2027, less than six months of relevant work experience and availability to begin in August or September 2027.

Visa lists an estimated annual salary of USD 116,480 and requires permanent U.S. work authorization.

Visa Leadership Associate Program 2027

The Visa Leadership Associate Program is another two-year graduate rotational pathway in the Bay Area.

Associates complete four six-month assignments designed around:

  • Client centricity
  • Product development
  • Financial and data acumen
  • Strategic thinking

Possible functions include Marketing, Fintech Partnerships, Product Management, Sales and Social Impact.

Visa lists an estimated salary of USD 95,680 and requires permanent U.S. authorization to work without sponsorship.

Software Engineer – New College Graduate, Bellevue

Visa is also recruiting 2027 new graduates for full-time software-engineering roles in Bellevue.

Candidates should normally have a bachelor’s or master’s degree in a relevant discipline, graduate between May 2026 and August 2027, and have less than six months of relevant professional experience.

The role lists an estimated annual salary of USD 114,400 and requires permanent U.S. work authorization.

Who Should Consider Applying?

Visa’s 2027 recruitment cycle is relevant to students and early-career professionals from a wide range of disciplines.

For technology opportunities, common backgrounds include:

  • Computer Science
  • Computer Engineering
  • Cybersecurity
  • Information Systems
  • Data Science
  • Mathematics
  • Statistics
  • Engineering

For commercial and product roles, relevant backgrounds can include:

  • Business Administration
  • Economics
  • Finance
  • Marketing
  • Communications
  • Management Information Systems
  • International Business
  • Operations
  • Product Management
  • Design

Visa frequently emphasizes that academic major is only one part of the candidate profile. Communication skills, analytical thinking, collaboration, curiosity, digital fluency and willingness to learn are recurring requirements across the current postings.

Digital and AI Skills Are Increasingly Important

A notable theme across Visa’s new U.S. postings is digital fluency.

Several current vacancies explicitly state that Visa employees should be able to work with emerging technologies, including generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, as part of everyday work.

Applicants therefore do not necessarily need to be AI specialists, but they may benefit from demonstrating responsible familiarity with AI-enabled productivity, research, analysis or development tools.

Work Authorization Is Critical

Students should not assume that Visa provides sponsorship simply because the company operates internationally.

For the newly opened U.S. internships reviewed here, Visa states that it will not sponsor applicants for employment visas and will not consider future sponsorship.

The U.S. new-graduate rotational programmes similarly require permanent authorization to work in the United States.

Country-specific requirements differ elsewhere. For example, the Dutch-speaking Amsterdam consulting internship requires full permanent right to work in the Netherlands and fluency in both Dutch and English.

Applicants should therefore read the work-authorization section of the specific vacancy before investing significant time in an application.

Application Deadline

For the newly launched U.S. 2027 internship and graduate recruitment cycle, Visa states in several postings that applications are accepted from:

17 September 2026 to 24 September 2026.

Some Workday pages display a formal system end date of:

25 September 2026.

Because the text of the vacancy itself identifies 24 September as the application window, applicants should submit by 24 September 2026 rather than relying on the later system date.

Other international internships have role-specific timelines and should be checked individually.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through Visa’s official Early Careers Workday portal.

Apply through Visa Early Careers

Candidates should search the exact job title, review:

  • Degree requirements
  • Graduation window
  • Location
  • Work authorization
  • Language requirements
  • Pay information where disclosed
  • Internship dates
  • Closing date

before applying.

How to Prepare a Strong Visa Internship Application

A strong application should demonstrate more than academic performance.

For a software-engineering role, applicants should make technical projects visible. That may include coursework, personal software projects, hackathons, GitHub work, engineering clubs or previous internships.

For an APM internship, candidates should demonstrate a mixture of customer thinking, analytical ability, product curiosity, communication and cross-functional collaboration.

For a sales internship, evidence of communication, leadership, customer service, campus involvement, research or team-based work can be valuable even without prior formal sales experience.

For consulting or analytics, candidates should emphasize structured problem solving, numerical analysis, presentation skills and an ability to turn data into recommendations.

For marketing, useful evidence may include campaign experience, consumer research, digital content, analytics, student organizations or event coordination.

Across roles, applicants should tailor their CV rather than sending the same document to every vacancy.

Key Information at a Glance

Organization: Visa

Recruitment cycle: 2027 Early Careers

Opportunity types: Internships, New College Graduate positions and rotational programmes

Fields: Software Engineering, Product Management, Sales, Consulting, Analytics, Marketing, Client Services, Strategy, Data and more

Main newly launched U.S. internship locations: Foster City, Atlanta, Bellevue and Austin

Other current portal locations include: Morocco, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Poland, Netherlands and Ukraine

Typical U.S. summer internship duration: Approximately 12 weeks

European summer programme examples: Approximately 11 weeks

U.S. internship graduation windows: Often December 2027–August 2028, depending on role

Sophomore programme graduation window: December 2028–August 2029

U.S. sponsorship: Not provided for the reviewed 2027 internships

Main U.S. recruitment deadline: Apply by 24 September 2026

Official portal:
Visa Early Careers

Conclusion

The Visa 2027 Internship and Early Careers recruitment cycle offers university students and recent graduates several distinct routes into one of the world’s largest payments and technology companies.

The newest U.S. openings include internships in Associate Product Management, Sales Development and Software Engineering, along with an early-entry Sophomore Software Engineering programme. Visa is simultaneously recruiting recent graduates into full-time rotational and technology programmes including the Associate Product Manager Program, Visa Leadership Associate Program and Software Engineer New College Graduate role.

The wider Visa Early Careers portal also currently contains internship opportunities across marketing, consulting, analytics, client services, data strategy and Value-Added Services in multiple international locations. Because the portal is dynamic and some older listings contain inconsistent internship dates, candidates should always open the specific vacancy and confirm that its programme dates and eligibility requirements remain applicable before submitting.

For students targeting the newly launched U.S. 2027 opportunities, the most important practical point is timing: Visa’s vacancy text identifies an application period running 17–24 September 2026, even though some Workday pages display 25 September as the system end date. Applying by 24 September 2026 is therefore the safer approach.

Visa’s internship programmes can provide much more than a short period of work experience. Several are explicitly designed as pipelines toward future internships or full-time graduate programmes, meaning a strong performance can potentially become an entry point into a longer-term career in technology, product, payments, consulting or commercial leadership.

To explore more global job opportunities, VISIT HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The University of Helsinki in Finland is inviting applications for a fixed-term Postdoctoral Researcher position focusing on climate democracy and community-based democratic responses to climate turbulence.

The position offers an opportunity for an early-career researcher to contribute to an interdisciplinary research project examining how communities and democratic institutions can respond to the climate crisis.

The successful candidate will work across environmental sciences and social sciences and will contribute to research involving areas such as deliberative assemblies, food and energy systems, disaster and climate adaptation responses, ecological urban design, environmental justice, and democratic innovations.

The position is connected to the Finnish Research Council Profi9-supported Climate Democracy project, led by Professor David Schlosberg, and is expected to begin in January 2027.

The appointment is initially for three years, with a possibility of extension depending on continued project funding and the continuation of the research programme.

Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate Democracy at University of Helsinki

The University of Helsinki is seeking a collaborative and proactive researcher to join its interdisciplinary Climate Democracy project.

The research position is based within either:

  • The Department of Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences; or
  • The Discipline of Social and Public Policy, Faculty of Social Sciences.

The project brings together environmental and social science perspectives to investigate democratic responses to climate turbulence and the ways communities can participate in developing responses to climate-related challenges.

The successful applicant will have the opportunity to conduct both independent and collaborative research while working with researchers, community organizations, project partners and international research networks.

About the Climate Democracy Project

The position is linked to a project supported by the Finnish Research Council Profi9 programme.

The Climate Democracy project is led by Professor David Schlosberg, whose research background includes environmental politics, environmental justice and democracy.

The project explores democratic and community-based responses to the climate crisis.

Rather than focusing only on the scientific or technological dimensions of climate change, the project examines how democratic processes, communities and institutions can contribute to responding to climate-related challenges.

The research may cover several interconnected areas, including:

  • Deliberative assemblies
  • Community-based democratic innovations
  • Food systems
  • Energy systems
  • Disaster response
  • Climate adaptation
  • Ecological urban design
  • Environmental justice
  • Political responses to climate change
  • Public participation
  • Community-based experiments
  • Democratic approaches to climate turbulence

This interdisciplinary focus means that candidates from different academic backgrounds may be considered, provided their research experience is relevant to the broader field of climate democracy.

Key Details of the Postdoctoral Position

  • Position: Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate Democracy
  • Research focus: Community-based democratic responses to climate turbulence
  • Institution: University of Helsinki
  • Country: Finland
  • Faculties: Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Faculty of Social Sciences
  • Possible departments: Department of Environmental Sciences or Discipline of Social and Public Policy
  • Project: Climate Democracy
  • Project leader: Professor David Schlosberg
  • Funding: Finnish Research Council Profi9 support
  • Contract: Fixed-term
  • Initial duration: Three years
  • Expected starting date: January 2027
  • Salary: Approximately €3,700–€4,000 per month at the start, depending on qualifications and experience
  • Working location: Helsinki, Finland
  • Campuses: City Centre or Viikki
  • Teaching: Approximately 10–20% of annual working time
  • Trial period: Six months
  • Application language: English
  • Application format: Single PDF
  • Deadline: 16 October 2026 at 23:59 EEST

What Will the Postdoctoral Researcher Do?

The successful candidate will have a broad research and project-management role.

The position is not limited to conducting individual academic research. The researcher will also contribute to the coordination, implementation and communication of activities within the wider Climate Democracy project.

Key responsibilities include the following.

1. Conduct Collaborative and Independent Research

The postdoctoral researcher will conduct research into community-based democratic innovations and experiments responding to the climate crisis.

This will involve working both independently and collaboratively with other researchers and project partners.

The successful candidate may therefore be expected to:

  • Develop research questions
  • Conduct academic research
  • Participate in collaborative research activities
  • Analyze democratic responses to climate change
  • Study community-based initiatives
  • Contribute to interdisciplinary research
  • Develop research outputs
  • Present findings to academic and public audiences

The position provides room for the researcher to develop their own research expertise while contributing to the objectives of the wider project.

2. Assess and Evaluate Community-Based Processes

Another important component of the role is the assessment and comparison of democratic processes and community-based responses to climate change.

The researcher will work with researchers and project partners to:

  • Design assessments
  • Conduct evaluations
  • Compare different processes
  • Examine community-based experiments
  • Analyze democratic innovations
  • Work with academic partners
  • Work with community-based partners

This aspect of the role is particularly relevant for candidates with experience in qualitative or quantitative research, evaluation, comparative research, public policy, environmental governance or related areas.

3. Coordinate and Manage Research Activities

The successful candidate will also contribute to project management.

Responsibilities include coordinating multiple researchers and managing specific research tasks within the Climate Democracy project.

This means the role requires more than academic research skills.

Candidates should also be able to:

  • Organize research activities
  • Coordinate researchers
  • Manage research tasks
  • Track project activities
  • Communicate with project partners
  • Meet project deadlines
  • Contribute to project planning
  • Support implementation of research activities

Experience with research project management is specifically identified as one of the requirements.

4. Publish Academic Research

The researcher will be expected to contribute to the project’s academic outputs.

This includes:

  • Writing peer-reviewed publications
  • Developing research articles
  • Contributing to collaborative publications
  • Developing research expertise
  • Preparing competitive grant applications

The university is therefore looking for a candidate with an emerging academic publication record and the potential to develop further as an independent researcher.

5. Prepare Project Documentation and Reports

The postdoctoral researcher will also support the preparation of project documentation.

This may include:

  • Research reports
  • Project documentation
  • Academic articles
  • Public-facing articles
  • Other written outputs

The role therefore requires strong writing skills and the ability to communicate research to audiences beyond academia.

6. Organize Seminars and Workshops

The successful candidate will take a leading role in organizing and promoting seminars and workshops associated with the research project.

Responsibilities may include:

  • Seminar planning
  • Workshop organization
  • Research event coordination
  • Communication
  • Logistics
  • Financial coordination
  • Web content
  • Social media content
  • Promotion of research activities

This makes communication and organizational skills important components of the position.

7. Build Research Networks

The researcher will also contribute to developing a broader community of researchers and practitioners.

The successful candidate will participate in:

  • Research seminars
  • Workshops
  • Academic discussions
  • Research networks
  • Collaborative activities
  • Engagement with Finnish partners
  • European research networks
  • International research networks

The position therefore provides opportunities to engage with researchers and practitioners both within Finland and internationally.

8. Teaching Responsibilities

Teaching may account for approximately 10–20% of annual working time.

This means the role combines research, project coordination, academic engagement and a limited teaching component.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to contribute to teaching activities in addition to their research responsibilities.

What Qualifications Are Required?

The University of Helsinki is looking for a candidate with an interdisciplinary interest in democratic and justice-based responses to the climate crisis.

The university specifically expects applicants to demonstrate several qualifications and experiences.

PhD Requirement

Applicants must have completed a PhD in an area related to climate democracy, broadly defined.

The relevant academic background can come from different disciplines, including:

  • Humanities
  • Social sciences
  • Natural sciences
  • Environmental sciences
  • Political science
  • Public policy
  • Environmental politics
  • Related interdisciplinary fields

Importantly, the doctoral degree requirement must be fulfilled by the beginning of employment.

Therefore, candidates who have not yet formally completed their PhD may potentially be considered if they will have met the degree requirement by the time the employment begins.

Knowledge of Climate-Related Issues

Applicants should demonstrate knowledge and an emerging research profile in one or more fields related to:

  • Climate crises
  • Climate democracy
  • Political responses to climate change
  • Public responses to climate change
  • Environmental justice
  • Democratic innovation
  • Climate adaptation
  • Community-based responses
  • Environmental governance
  • Related areas

The university describes climate democracy broadly, meaning applicants do not necessarily need to come from one narrowly defined discipline.

Independent Research Experience

Applicants should demonstrate their ability to conduct independent research.

This includes evidence that the candidate can:

  • Develop research ideas
  • Conduct research independently
  • Take responsibility for research projects
  • Complete research activities
  • Produce academic publications
  • Develop their research expertise

Candidates should therefore be able to demonstrate their research independence through their doctoral work, publications, projects or other relevant academic experience.

Academic Publication Record

Applicants should have an emerging track record in academic publications.

The university also emphasizes the potential to develop further research expertise through participation in different projects.

Candidates should therefore highlight relevant publications and research outputs in their CV and motivation letter.

Where applicable, applicants can demonstrate their experience through:

  • Peer-reviewed journal articles
  • Book chapters
  • Research reports
  • Conference papers
  • Collaborative publications
  • Other relevant academic outputs

Project Management Experience

Experience in project management is specifically required.

Candidates should be able to demonstrate experience managing or coordinating research activities, projects, teams or related initiatives.

Relevant experience may include:

  • Research project coordination
  • Managing project timelines
  • Coordinating researchers
  • Organizing workshops
  • Managing research events
  • Coordinating partners
  • Grant project administration
  • Research programme management

Collaborative Working Skills

The university is seeking a person who can work collaboratively.

The successful researcher will interact with:

  • Academic researchers
  • Community organizations
  • Project partners
  • Research networks
  • Finnish institutions
  • European partners
  • International researchers and practitioners

Applicants should therefore demonstrate experience working effectively in collaborative environments.

International and Multidisciplinary Experience

Experience working in international and/or multidisciplinary settings is also expected.

This is particularly relevant because the project brings together environmental and social science perspectives and involves collaboration with Finnish, European and international partners.

Applicants should highlight relevant international research collaborations, multidisciplinary projects, academic networks or cross-sector research experiences where applicable.

English Language Requirement

Applicants must have excellent written and spoken English.

This is important because the role involves:

  • Academic writing
  • Peer-reviewed publications
  • Grant applications
  • Research presentations
  • Workshops
  • Seminars
  • Project documentation
  • Communication with international partners

The application itself must also be submitted in English.

Salary and Employment Conditions

The position is offered as a fixed-term three-year appointment.

The preferred starting date is January 2027, depending on practical arrangements.

The salary is based on level 5 of the demands level chart for teaching and research personnel in the Finnish university salary system.

In addition to the basic salary component, the appointee will receive a salary component based on personal performance.

The starting salary is typically approximately:

€3,700–€4,000 per month

The exact starting salary will depend on the successful candidate’s:

  • Qualifications
  • Experience
  • Academic profile
  • Relevant expertise

A six-month trial period will apply.

Where Will the Researcher Work?

The successful applicant is expected to reside in Finland while employed by the University of Helsinki.

The position will be based in Helsinki, at either:

  • City Centre Campus, or
  • Viikki Campus

The researcher will join either the Department of Environmental Sciences in the Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences or the Discipline of Social and Public Policy in the Faculty of Social Sciences.

Working Environment at the University of Helsinki

The University of Helsinki describes its working environment as international and multidisciplinary.

The successful candidate will have opportunities to collaborate with researchers and partners across environmental and social sciences.

The Climate Democracy project connects researchers working in different fields and provides opportunities to participate in:

  • Research seminars
  • Workshops
  • Academic networks
  • Finnish research collaborations
  • European partnerships
  • International research networks

The position can therefore provide a platform for an early-career researcher to develop both their academic profile and international research network.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their application as one PDF file in English through the University of Helsinki Recruitment System.

The application should contain the following documents:

1. Motivation Letter

A motivation letter of maximum two pages is required.

The letter should explain the applicant’s suitability for the position and demonstrate their interest in the Climate Democracy project.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants should provide an up-to-date CV detailing their:

  • Academic qualifications
  • Research experience
  • Publications
  • Project experience
  • International experience
  • Multidisciplinary work
  • Relevant professional experience

3. Relevant Certificates or Transcripts

Applicants should include relevant academic documentation, such as:

  • Doctoral diploma
  • Academic certificates
  • Transcripts

Candidates should provide documentation relevant to their eligibility for the position.

4. Contact Information for Two References

Applicants must provide contact information for two references.

Applicants should ensure that the reference details are accurate and that the referees are appropriate for an academic postdoctoral application.

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications is:

16 October 2026 at 23:59 EEST

Applicants should make sure their complete application is submitted before the stated deadline.

Because the application requires a motivation letter, CV, academic documentation and two references, candidates should allow sufficient time to prepare and combine all documents into the required single PDF.

Who Should Apply?

This position is particularly relevant to researchers who have recently completed, or will complete by the employment start date, a PhD in a field connected to climate democracy or related climate, environmental, social science, humanities or natural science disciplines.

Potentially relevant backgrounds include:

  • Environmental politics
  • Environmental science
  • Political science
  • Public policy
  • Social sciences
  • Environmental sociology
  • Sustainability studies
  • Climate adaptation
  • Environmental justice
  • Geography
  • Political ecology
  • Governance
  • Democracy studies
  • Urban sustainability
  • Food systems
  • Energy systems
  • Disaster studies
  • Related humanities or natural science fields

However, the university defines climate democracy broadly, so applicants should assess their fit based on their research expertise and demonstrated connection to the project’s themes, rather than relying solely on their degree title.

International Applicants

The announcement encourages qualified applicants from diverse backgrounds to apply.

The position is based at the University of Helsinki in Finland, and the successful candidate is expected to reside in Finland during employment.

The announcement does not restrict applications to Finnish citizens or to applicants from a particular nationality or continent.

Therefore, qualified international researchers can apply, subject to the University’s employment requirements and any applicable Finnish immigration and residence requirements.

The announcement specifically emphasizes an inclusive university community and encourages qualified candidates from diverse backgrounds.

Why This Position Is Significant for Early-Career Researchers

This postdoctoral position combines several elements that can be valuable for researchers seeking to develop an independent academic profile.

The researcher will have opportunities to:

  • Conduct independent research
  • Participate in collaborative interdisciplinary research
  • Publish academic work
  • Develop grant applications
  • Manage research activities
  • Coordinate researchers
  • Work with community-based partners
  • Organize academic workshops and seminars
  • Engage with international research networks
  • Develop experience in public-facing research communication
  • Contribute to teaching

The position therefore extends beyond a narrowly defined postdoctoral research assignment and includes research coordination, project management, communication and academic networking.

Click HERE to read more.

Research Themes Covered by the Position

The climate democracy research area is broad and may involve several interconnected themes.

These include:

Deliberative Assemblies

Research may examine how deliberative democratic processes can be used to engage communities and citizens in decisions relating to climate change and environmental policy.

Food Systems

The project may explore democratic and community-based approaches to food systems and their relationship with climate change and sustainability.

Energy Systems

Research may examine democratic participation and community responses related to energy systems and the transition toward more sustainable energy.

Disaster and Adaptation Response

The position can involve research into how communities and democratic institutions respond to climate-related disasters and adaptation challenges.

Ecological Urban Design

Research may also address how democratic processes and community participation can contribute to urban environments designed around ecological and climate considerations.

Environmental Justice

Environmental justice is another important dimension of the position, particularly in understanding how climate responses affect different communities and how democratic approaches can address questions of equity and justice.

Diversity and Inclusion

The University of Helsinki states that a diverse and equitable study and work culture is important to the institution.

The university indicates that it seeks to promote an inclusive university community and encourages qualified applicants from diverse backgrounds to apply.

This means the opportunity is open to qualified researchers without the announcement specifying a nationality, ethnicity or racial restriction.

Applicants should nevertheless satisfy the academic, research and professional requirements outlined in the vacancy.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate Democracy position at the University of Helsinki provides an opportunity for an early-career researcher to contribute to interdisciplinary research on democratic and community-based responses to the climate crisis.

The project covers a broad range of themes, including deliberative democracy, food and energy systems, disaster and climate adaptation, ecological urban design and environmental justice. The successful researcher will combine independent and collaborative research with project management, academic publishing, grant development, workshops, seminars, research communication and limited teaching responsibilities.

Applicants should have a PhD in a field related to climate democracy or the climate crisis, an emerging publication record, independent research experience, project-management skills, collaborative experience and excellent English-language abilities. Experience in international or multidisciplinary environments is also expected.

The position is initially offered for three years, with a preferred start in January 2027, and offers a starting salary of approximately €3,700–€4,000 per month, depending on qualifications and experience.

Qualified researchers from diverse backgrounds and international applicants can apply, provided they meet the stated requirements and are able to satisfy the employment and residence requirements associated with the position in Finland.

Interested candidates should prepare a maximum two-page motivation letter, CV, relevant academic certificates or transcripts, and contact information for two references, combine these materials into a single PDF in English, and submit the application through the University of Helsinki Recruitment System before 16 October 2026 at 23:59 EEST.

Click HERE for more job opportunities.
