item.content:encoded:
The Global Environment Facility Small Grants Programme (GEF SGP), implemented by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Ghana, has announced the 2nd Call for Proposals under the Global Support Initiative on Territories and Areas Conserved by Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (ICCA-GSI) Phase II.

The 2026 call is designed to support community-led conservation, biodiversity protection, sustainable livelihoods, climate resilience, sustainable agriculture and fisheries, low-carbon development, chemicals and waste management, and sustainable urban solutions in Ghana.

Through this call, eligible local organizations and community-based groups can apply for grants of up to US$50,000 to implement innovative initiatives that contribute to the goals of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and strengthen the recognition and effectiveness of territories and areas conserved by Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities.

This opportunity is particularly relevant for NGOs, civil society organizations, community-based organizations, community groups and eligible social enterprises operating in Ghana, especially those working in the priority areas identified under the programme.

Opportunity Overview

The ICCA-GSI Phase II call is part of the GEF Small Grants Programme Operational Phase 8 (OP8) in Ghana. It seeks organizations capable of implementing locally driven solutions that strengthen biodiversity conservation while simultaneously improving livelihoods and community resilience.

The programme recognizes that Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities play an important role in conserving ecosystems through customary governance systems, traditional knowledge and community-led environmental management.

Under the 2026 call, applicants can submit proposals addressing one or more of five strategic initiative areas.

About the ICCA-GSI Phase II Programme

The Global Support Initiative on Territories and Areas Conserved by Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (GSI-ICCA) is a flagship initiative under the GEF Small Grants Programme.

The initiative is implemented by UNDP and focuses on strengthening the contribution of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities to:

  • Biodiversity conservation
  • Sustainable livelihoods
  • Climate resilience
  • Ecosystem protection
  • Community governance
  • Sustainable natural-resource management
  • Environmental policy engagement
  • Knowledge sharing

The programme is based on the recognition that communities living in and around important ecosystems can play a central role in protecting biodiversity and managing natural resources sustainably.

ICCA-GSI therefore supports locally driven approaches rather than relying solely on externally designed conservation interventions.

According to the programme information, ICCAs cover nearly one-third of the world’s land and make significant contributions to biodiversity conservation and community wellbeing.

The initiative is funded by the Government of Germany through its Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, Nuclear Safety and Consumer Protection (BMUV).

It also contributes to the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), particularly Targets 3, 21, 22 and 23.

What Is the 2026 Call for Proposals About?

The 2026 call is described as a two-in-one Call for Proposals. It provides opportunities for organizations to undertake different types of work under the ICCA-GSI Phase II programme.

There are two separate assignments:

1. Catalytic NGO – Monitoring and Evaluation

The first opportunity is intended for a Catalytic NGO that will support monitoring and evaluation activities based on the ICCA-GSI methodology and tools.

This component focuses on strengthening the monitoring, evaluation and learning processes associated with ICCA-GSI interventions.

Applicants interested in this assignment should use the designated Catalytic NGO proposal template provided by UNDP Ghana.

2. Community-Based NGOs/CSOs – Regular Project Grants

The second opportunity provides regular project grants for community-based NGOs and civil society organizations.

These organizations are expected to implement community-led projects that contribute to the achievement of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and align with the objectives of the ICCA programme.

Applicants for this component should use the designated Regular Projects Grants proposal template.

Organizations should carefully review the relevant call document and use the correct application template for the assignment they are applying for.

Priority Geographic Areas

Geographic targeting is an important component of this funding opportunity.

The call prioritizes communities along the Black Volta Basin, particularly communities located in the following districts and municipality:

Upper West Region

  • Wa-West District

Bono Region

  • Banda District

Savannah Region

  • Bole District
  • Sawla-Tuna-Kalba District
  • Central Gonja Municipality

Organizations planning to apply should therefore carefully consider the geographic eligibility requirements and ensure that their proposed activities correspond with the programme’s identified priority areas.

A proposal may have a strong environmental concept, but applicants should still demonstrate alignment with the geographic priorities and objectives of the ICCA-GSI Phase II programme.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is primarily intended for organizations and community groups operating in Ghana that meet the eligibility requirements established by UNDP Ghana.

Eligible applicants include:

  • Local non-governmental organizations
  • Non-profit organizations
  • Civil society organizations
  • Community-based organizations
  • Community groups
  • Eligible social enterprise organizations

The call specifically states that organizations must satisfy the applicable registration, recognition and documentation requirements.

Organizational Eligibility Requirements

For local NGOs and non-profit organizations, applicants should have valid documentation from the relevant authorities, including:

  • Registrar General’s Department certification
  • Social Welfare certification

Community groups and community-based organizations may also be eligible where they are appropriately recognized by the relevant authorities.

Social enterprise organizations may be eligible where they are recognized by the relevant District Assemblies and the Environmental Protection Agency of Ghana.

Applicants should consult the official call documentation for the complete eligibility conditions because registration status alone may not be sufficient to establish eligibility.

What Types of Projects Are Relevant?

The strongest alignment will come from projects that connect community leadership with environmental and development outcomes.

Relevant project concepts could include initiatives addressing:

Biodiversity

  • Threatened species
  • Ecosystem conservation
  • Habitat protection
  • Biodiversity restoration
  • Community conservation

Climate Resilience

  • Climate-resilient livelihoods
  • Community adaptation
  • Ecosystem-based resilience
  • Sustainable resource management

Sustainable Livelihoods

  • Sustainable agriculture
  • Sustainable fisheries
  • Community enterprises
  • Natural-resource-based livelihoods
  • Food security

Environmental Management

  • Waste management
  • Chemicals management
  • Pollution reduction
  • Sustainable resource use

Energy

  • Low-carbon energy
  • Renewable energy access
  • Community energy solutions

Urban Sustainability

  • Sustainable urban planning
  • Government-CSO-private-sector collaboration
  • Environmental policy dialogue
  • Community participation in urban solutions

Alignment With the Global Biodiversity Framework

A significant component of the regular project grants is alignment with the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF).

The GBF provides an international framework for addressing biodiversity loss and strengthening conservation and sustainable use.

Under this call, community-led projects are expected to contribute to the broader biodiversity objectives of the framework while remaining aligned with the ICCA programme.

The call particularly references GBF Targets:

  • Target 3
  • Target 21
  • Target 22
  • Target 23

Applicants should therefore consider how their proposed project contributes to biodiversity conservation, participation, knowledge, rights, equity and community involvement within the relevant framework.

Why Community Leadership Is Central to the Programme

ICCA-GSI is built around the recognition that communities are not simply beneficiaries of conservation projects.

Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities can also be important decision-makers, custodians of traditional knowledge and managers of natural resources.

Community-led conservation can help connect:

  • Local knowledge
  • Traditional governance
  • Biodiversity conservation
  • Sustainable livelihoods
  • Climate adaptation
  • Environmental management
  • Community participation

This makes community ownership an important consideration when developing a proposal.

Applicants should clearly explain the role that communities will play in identifying problems, designing interventions, implementing activities and monitoring results.

What Should Applicants Consider When Preparing a Proposal?

Organizations preparing an application should ensure that the proposed project is clearly connected to the objectives of the call.

Important considerations include:

1. Define the environmental or community problem

Clearly explain the issue that the project intends to address.

For example, this could involve:

  • Biodiversity loss
  • Ecosystem degradation
  • Unsustainable resource use
  • Climate vulnerability
  • Food insecurity
  • Waste management challenges
  • Limited access to sustainable energy

2. Identify the communities involved

Explain who will participate and who will benefit.

The proposal should make community participation clear rather than presenting a project that is designed and implemented entirely externally.

3. Connect the project to the strategic areas

Applicants should clearly demonstrate which of the five strategic initiative areas their project addresses.

4. Demonstrate geographic relevance

Where applicable, demonstrate how the project relates to the priority geographic areas identified by the call.

5. Explain the expected results

A strong proposal should clearly communicate what will change as a result of the project.

Expected results could involve:

  • Improved ecosystem protection
  • Increased biodiversity conservation
  • Improved livelihoods
  • Greater climate resilience
  • Better waste management
  • Increased sustainable energy access
  • Stronger environmental governance

6. Demonstrate sustainability

Applicants should consider what happens after the grant period ends.

The proposal should explain how project benefits, community structures, knowledge or conservation activities can continue over time.

Proposal Workshop

UNDP Ghana will organize a virtual proposal workshop on Tuesday, 22 September 2026.

The workshop is intended to provide additional information about the proposal process and the call.

Applicants should consult the official Call for Proposals for the workshop details, including the participation information and any instructions provided by UNDP.

Organizations considering applying should take advantage of the workshop where possible because it can provide additional clarification about the application process.

How to Apply

Eligible organizations should prepare their applications using the appropriate proposal template.

There are separate templates for the two assignments:

For the Catalytic NGO Assignment

Applicants should use the designated Catalytic NGO proposal template for monitoring and evaluation activities based on the ICCA-GSI methodology and tools.

For Regular Project Grants

Community-based NGOs and CSOs applying for project implementation should use the designated Regular Projects Grants proposal template.

Applicants should ensure that they are using the correct template before submitting their proposal.

About the GEF Small Grants Programme

The Global Environment Facility Small Grants Programme (GEF SGP) supports locally driven initiatives addressing environmental and sustainable development challenges.

The programme places significant emphasis on community-level action and partnerships with civil society and local organizations.

Through its small-grants approach, the programme can support organizations working on issues such as:

  • Biodiversity
  • Climate change
  • Land degradation
  • International waters
  • Chemicals and waste
  • Sustainable livelihoods
  • Community resilience

The Ghana ICCA-GSI call is therefore part of a broader global environmental funding mechanism.

About UNDP Ghana

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is implementing the GEF Small Grants Programme in Ghana.

Under the ICCA-GSI initiative, UNDP works to strengthen the recognition and effectiveness of territories and areas conserved by Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities.

The Ghana programme connects local community action with national and global environmental priorities.

About ICCAs

Indigenous and Community Conserved Areas (ICCAs) refer broadly to territories and areas where Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities have a strong relationship with the land and natural resources and play a significant role in conservation and governance.

These areas can contribute to:

  • Biodiversity conservation
  • Ecosystem protection
  • Sustainable livelihoods
  • Cultural continuity
  • Traditional knowledge
  • Climate resilience
  • Community wellbeing

The ICCA-GSI programme seeks to strengthen the enabling environment and practical capacity for these community-led conservation systems.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be relevant to organizations in Ghana that are already working in areas such as:

  • Biodiversity conservation

  • Food security

  • Sustainable energy
  • Urban sustainability
  • Community governance
  • Indigenous and local-community conservation

Organizations should, however, confirm their eligibility against the official call before investing significant time in proposal preparation.

Conclusion

The 2nd Call for Proposals – Community-Led Conservation under ICCA-GSI Phase II 2026 provides an opportunity for eligible organizations and community groups in Ghana to obtain funding for locally driven environmental and community development initiatives.

With grants of up to US$50,000, the programme covers five broad strategic areas: community-based conservation of threatened ecosystems and species; sustainable agriculture, fisheries and food security; low-carbon energy access; chemicals and waste management; and sustainable urban solutions.

The call places particular emphasis on communities along the Black Volta Basin, including priority areas in the Upper West, Bono and Savannah Regions.

Eligible applicants should carefully review the relevant UNDP Ghana call document, select the appropriate proposal template, ensure that their project fits the programme’s geographic and thematic priorities, and submit their application electronically by 3 October 2026 at 5:00 PM.

The opportunity is particularly relevant for Ghanaian NGOs, CSOs, community-based organizations, community groups and eligible social enterprises seeking to combine community leadership, biodiversity conservation, sustainable livelihoods and climate resilience in practical local projects.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children 2026, an international gathering designed to place young people and survivor advocates at the centre of global conversations about preventing and ending violence against children.

The Summit will take place on 15–16 November 2026 in Manila, Philippines, at the Marriott Manila Hotel. It will bring together young people, survivor leaders, advocates and other stakeholders to exchange experiences, develop policy recommendations, strengthen networks and influence international action on ending violence against children.

The event is being organised ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, which will also take place in Manila in November 2026. This positioning gives participants an important opportunity to contribute youth- and survivor-led perspectives at a time when governments, international organisations and civil society actors will be discussing how to accelerate global progress on child protection.

About the Global Youth & Survivor Summit 2026

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is intended to provide a dedicated platform where young people and people with lived experience can help shape the international agenda for ending violence against children.

Rather than treating young people and survivors simply as participants in discussions led by institutions, the Summit is structured around their leadership, perspectives and experiences. The organisers want young people and survivor advocates to engage directly with policymakers, donors, civil society organisations, faith-based organisations and other actors working on child protection.

The Summit comes at a critical time. According to the organisers, an estimated one billion children around the world experience some form of violence every year. At the same time, governments and other stakeholders have made hundreds of commitments aimed at strengthening child protection.

The challenge is therefore not limited to obtaining new commitments. It also involves ensuring that existing pledges are translated into meaningful, sustained and accountable action — with the people most affected by these issues involved in determining what effective action should look like.

Summit Dates and Location

The main event details are:

  • Event: Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children
  • Dates: 15–16 November 2026
  • Venue: Marriott Manila Hotel
  • Location: Manila, Philippines
  • Working language: English
  • Application deadline: 25 September 2026
  • Deadline time: 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8)
  • Registration fee: None

Interpretation support may be considered depending on the needs of confirmed participants and the availability of appropriate resources.

What Is the Purpose of the Youth & Survivor Summit?

The Summit has been developed to strengthen the role that young people and survivor advocates play in international efforts to end violence against children.

One of its central objectives is to gather policy recommendations directly from young people and survivor advocates. These recommendations can contribute to wider discussions taking place around the Second Global Ministerial Conference.

The Summit is also expected to help participants establish stronger connections with youth-led and survivor-led organisations, networks and movements operating in different parts of the world.

Broadly, the event focuses on three interconnected objectives.

1. Strengthening Global Connections and Solidarity

Youth- and survivor-led organisations often work within different communities, countries and policy environments. The Summit aims to connect these networks and create opportunities for longer-term collaboration.

Participants will have opportunities to meet other advocates, exchange approaches, identify shared priorities and explore possibilities for collective advocacy beyond the event itself.

The intention is therefore not simply to organise a two-day meeting in Manila, but to strengthen relationships that can continue after participants return to their respective communities and organisations.

2. Putting Youth and Survivor Leadership at the Centre

A defining feature of the Summit is its focus on ensuring that people affected by violence against children have opportunities to influence discussions about the policies and programmes designed to address it.

Young people and survivor advocates will be able to share experiences, research, solutions and recommendations while engaging with decision-makers, funders and other stakeholders.

This approach is intended to move beyond symbolic participation and towards meaningful involvement in policy discussions and advocacy efforts.

The Summit therefore provides a platform for participants to contribute not only personal perspectives but also practical ideas about how governments, organisations and communities can strengthen the prevention of violence against children.

3. Turning Shared Priorities into Collective Action

The organisers also want the Summit to translate discussions into common priorities and calls for action.

By identifying areas where youth leaders, survivors and child-protection advocates have shared concerns, participants can develop stronger collective messages that may subsequently be used for advocacy, accountability and engagement with decision-makers.

These priorities are expected to support continued action beyond Manila rather than ending when the Summit concludes.

What Participants Can Expect

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is designed as an interactive space rather than a conventional conference dominated entirely by formal presentations.

Participants can expect opportunities to:

  • Connect with youth leaders and survivor advocates from different communities and backgrounds.
  • Exchange experiences and perspectives related to preventing violence against children.
  • Share research, community-based solutions and advocacy approaches.
  • Discuss policy priorities with other participants and stakeholders.
  • Contribute ideas that may influence wider discussions surrounding the Global Ministerial Conference.
  • Strengthen international networks and solidarity among youth- and survivor-led movements.
  • Participate in cross-generational dialogue with policymakers, donors, civil society representatives and other actors.
  • Develop collective priorities and advocacy messages for continued action after the Summit.

Restless Development has also highlighted leadership development and meaningful dialogue as important elements of the gathering.

Connection With the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children

The Youth & Survivor Summit is taking place immediately before the broader international discussions associated with the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children.

The official Ministerial Conference is scheduled for 18–19 November 2026 in Manila and is co-organised by the Government of the Philippines, World Health Organization and UNICEF, in collaboration with the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General on Violence Against Children.

The Ministerial Conference will bring together governments and a broad range of international stakeholders to accelerate action against violence affecting children.

Its agenda includes prevention-focused approaches such as support for parents and caregivers, safer schools and stronger response systems. Attention will also be given to emerging and escalating concerns including technology-facilitated violence, humanitarian and climate-related contexts, and the relationship between violence against children and violence against women.

The Youth & Survivor Summit is intended to make sure that youth and survivor perspectives contribute to this wider global moment.

However, applicants should understand an important distinction:

Selection for the Youth & Survivor Summit does not automatically provide access to the Second Global Ministerial Conference.

Participation and registration for the two events are separate. Being accepted to the Youth & Survivor Summit should therefore not be interpreted as an invitation to attend the official Ministerial Conference.

Is the Global Youth & Survivor Summit Fully Funded?

There is no registration fee to participate in the Summit.

Meals and refreshments during the official programme will also be provided.

However, the standard participation arrangement does not automatically cover international travel and other attendance expenses.

Unless an applicant receives a fully funded place, participants or their supporting organisations are responsible for costs including:

  • International or domestic travel
  • Accommodation
  • Visa expenses
  • Travel insurance
  • Local transportation
  • Personal expenses

The organisers have confirmed that a limited number of fully funded places are available for participants aged 18 and above who would otherwise be unable to attend the Summit.

These funded places are not guaranteed. Funding decisions will depend on eligibility, individual circumstances, demonstrated support needs and the amount of funding available to the organisers.

Applicants who require financial support should therefore clearly and accurately explain their circumstances when completing the application.

Special Conditions for Applicants Aged 15–17

Applicants aged 15 to 17 years are permitted to participate, but specific safeguarding requirements apply.

Anyone in this age group must be:

  1. Nominated by a partner organisation;
  2. Fully funded by that organisation; and
  3. Fully supported by the organisation for participation in the Summit.

Therefore, applicants between 15 and 17 cannot rely on the Summit’s limited funding mechanism available to participants aged 18 and above. Appropriate organisational support must already be in place.

How Will Applications Be Assessed?

Submitting an application does not guarantee that an applicant will receive a place.

The Summit Organising Committee will review applications while considering available capacity and several selection factors.

According to the official application information, these factors include:

  • Diversity and representation
  • Applicant motivation
  • Relevant experience
  • Potential contribution to the Summit
  • Individual support requirements
  • Availability of places

Applicants should therefore use the application form to demonstrate why participation is relevant to their experience, advocacy, community work or professional activities and how they could contribute meaningfully to discussions.

Applicants with relevant lived experience, youth leadership activities, child-protection advocacy, community organising, policy work, research or similar experience should clearly explain that background rather than providing only general statements about their interest in attending.

Safeguarding and Mental Health Support

Given the sensitive subject matter of violence against children and the involvement of people with lived experience, safeguarding forms an important part of the Summit.

The organisers state that they intend to create an environment that is safe, inclusive and respectful for participants irrespective of characteristics including age, gender, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation or disability.

Sessions and activities are intended to follow trauma-informed approaches.

Participants, speakers and partners will also be invited to participate in a safeguarding briefing before the Summit.

During the event, participants are expected to have access to:

  • On-site mental health support
  • First-aid support
  • A wellbeing space where participants can step away and decompress when necessary
  • Identifiable Summit team members who can respond to safeguarding concerns
  • A mechanism for confidential or anonymous reporting of concerns

These provisions are particularly significant for a conference involving survivors and potentially sensitive discussions about violence, exploitation, abuse and child protection.

Who Is Organising the Summit?

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is co-organised by:

  • Restless Development
  • Brave Movement
  • Global Youth-Led Movement on Ending Violence Against Children

The event is also being guided by a Summit Organising Committee composed of young advocates and professionals with experience across areas including human rights, survivor advocacy, public policy, child protection, youth participation, gender equality, communications, research and community-based development.

Why This Summit Matters

Violence against children is a global challenge that intersects with education, health, justice, gender equality, technology, humanitarian crises, social protection and human rights.

Effective solutions require more than institutional discussions between governments and development organisations. Young people and survivors can provide perspectives about how policies and interventions operate in practice, where protection systems fail and what changes communities actually need.

By providing a dedicated platform for youth and survivor leadership immediately before a major international Ministerial Conference, the Global Youth & Survivor Summit offers participants an opportunity to connect grassroots experience with international policy dialogue.

For young advocates, survivor leaders and people working to protect children, the Summit can therefore serve as both a global networking platform and a space for substantive advocacy.

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted by:

25 September 2026 at 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8).

Applications received after the deadline should not be assumed to be considered, so interested candidates are encouraged to complete the official form before the closing time.

Apply for the Global Youth & Survivor Summit 2026

Applicants can also review the official Summit information before submitting an application.

Visit the Official Youth & Survivor Summit Website

Conclusion

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children 2026 provides an important international platform for young people, survivor leaders and child-protection advocates to participate directly in discussions that affect children and communities worldwide.

Taking place in Manila, Philippines, on 15–16 November 2026, the Summit will create opportunities for participants to build international connections, exchange evidence and lived experiences, develop shared priorities and contribute to advocacy surrounding global efforts to end violence against children.

With no registration fee and a limited number of fully funded opportunities available for eligible participants aged 18 and above, the Summit may be particularly valuable for youth and survivor advocates who would otherwise have limited access to high-level international forums.

Interested applicants should carefully review the eligibility and funding requirements and submit their application no later than 25 September 2026 at 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8).

For more global opportunities, click HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program is inviting applications from researchers whose work aligns with the mission of the Bloomberg Center for Cities at Harvard University. The program supports rigorous, policy-relevant research focused on urban problem-solving and city leadership, with the aim of strengthening both academic scholarship and practical approaches to challenges facing cities.

Selected applicants will be appointed as Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars and will have the opportunity to spend either one semester or one full academic year in residence at the Bloomberg Center for Cities at Harvard University.

The program is designed to provide scholars with protected time to advance a specific research project while also participating in the intellectual community of the Center and contributing to selected academic activities.

Application Deadline: October 28, 2026

About the Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program

The Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program is a new visiting scholar initiative of the Bloomberg Center for Cities at Harvard University.

The program seeks to build a lasting and collaborative community of researchers whose work can contribute to the practice of urban problem-solving and city leadership.

The program is particularly interested in research that can help cities and city leaders strengthen their capacity to:

  • Drive performance
  • Lead innovation
  • Deliver results for residents
  • Develop effective policies
  • Strengthen organizational capabilities
  • Use evidence and data effectively
  • Collaborate across sectors

The program therefore provides an opportunity for researchers to pursue rigorous research while engaging with a community focused on translating knowledge into better urban governance and outcomes.

What Is the Bloomberg Center for Cities?

The Bloomberg Center for Cities at Harvard University supports research and learning focused on helping cities and city leaders improve their ability to deliver results.

The Center’s interests extend across different dimensions of city leadership, management, organizational performance, innovation, evidence-based policymaking, data, artificial intelligence, and cross-sector collaboration.

The Visiting Scholars Program is intended to contribute to this broader mission by bringing researchers into the Center’s intellectual community for a dedicated period of research.

Research Areas of Interest

The Bloomberg Center for Cities supports research addressing significant questions related to urban problem-solving and city leadership.

Areas of particular interest include, but are not limited to:

1. Mayoral Leadership and Management Strategies

Research may examine how mayors and other city leaders manage organizations, implement priorities, lead change, and deliver results.

Applicants working on leadership and management approaches within cities may find alignment with this area of interest.

2. High-Performing Staff and Teams

Another area of interest is understanding the conditions that enable high-performing staff and teams.

Research could examine organizational environments, management practices, leadership approaches, or other factors that contribute to effective public-sector teams.

3. Organizational Capabilities for Innovation

The program is also interested in research examining how organizations develop the capabilities needed to innovate.

This can include questions surrounding organizational structures, leadership, management, processes, and other conditions that support innovation in city government.

4. Evidence-Based Policy Solutions

The Center is interested in evidence-based policy solutions and the capacity required to implement and deliver them.

This creates an opportunity for researchers to examine not only which policies work, but also the institutional and organizational capabilities needed to put those policies into practice.

5. Data and Artificial Intelligence

The use of data and artificial intelligence to strengthen decision-making is another area of particular interest.

Researchers may explore how data and AI can support better decision-making in urban environments.

6. Cross-Sector Collaboration

The program also highlights effective approaches to cross-sector collaboration.

Research in this area may examine how governments, organizations, communities, and other actors can work together to address complex urban challenges.

These areas are not presented as an exhaustive list. The broader focus is on research that advances understanding and practice in urban problem-solving and city leadership.

Program Structure

The Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program is designed primarily to provide scholars with protected time for research.

During their residency, selected scholars will focus primarily on advancing the research project described in their application.

The residency can last for either:

  • One semester, or
  • One full academic year

This flexibility allows selected scholars to participate in the program for a period that fits the scope of their research and individual circumstances.

Research Focus During the Residency

The central purpose of the residency is to give scholars dedicated time to develop their proposed research.

The research project should be clearly defined in the application and should address a meaningful challenge related to urban problem-solving or city leadership.

While research will be the primary focus, scholars will also be expected to contribute to the intellectual life of the Bloomberg Center for Cities through a limited number of structured activities.

Activities and Expectations for Visiting Scholars

In addition to their research, Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars will participate in several activities during their residency.

Research Seminar

Scholars will be expected to host one research seminar per semester.

The seminar should focus on the scholar’s ongoing research or related themes.

This provides an opportunity to share research with members of the Center’s intellectual community and receive discussion and feedback.

Student Study Group

Scholars will also be expected to convene a student study group connected to their research.

The study group will:

  • Meet twice per month
  • Include monthly office hours
  • Facilitate discussion related to the scholar’s research

The study group is intended to facilitate discussion rather than function as formal classroom instruction.

Harvard Community Event

Each scholar will also organize one event, such as a talk or panel, that is open to the broader Harvard community.

This provides another opportunity for scholars to share ideas and engage with the wider university community.

Housing and Financial Support

The program provides housing near Harvard University for participating scholars.

In addition, financial assistance is available to help scholars dedicate sustained time to their proposed research project.

Depending on an individual scholar’s circumstances, financial support may be used to facilitate:

  • Course buyout
  • Other arrangements that allow the scholar to step back from regular academic obligations
  • Dedicated time to focus on the proposed research

The purpose of this support is to help selected scholars create sufficient protected time to advance their research during the residency.

Visa Support

The Bloomberg Center for Cities anticipates being able to sponsor visas for selected scholars, subject to:

  • Institutional policies
  • The individual scholar’s circumstances

International applicants should therefore consider the applicable visa and institutional requirements as part of the residency planning process.

Who Can Apply?

The program invites applications from researchers whose work aligns with the mission of the Bloomberg Center for Cities.

Applicants may come from:

  • Different disciplinary backgrounds
  • Different career stages

The program therefore does not restrict applicants to a single academic discipline, provided their research aligns with the Center’s mission and interests.

Academic Requirement

Applicants must hold a:

Doctoral degree (Ph.D. or comparable terminal research degree).

This is a core eligibility requirement for the program.

Current Academic or Research Appointment

At the time of application, applicants must also hold a current faculty or research appointment at one of the following:

  • A degree-granting university, or
  • A recognized research institution

Therefore, holding a doctoral degree alone is not sufficient. Applicants must also have a current qualifying faculty or research appointment when they apply.

Research Proposal Requirements

Applicants must submit a proposal describing the specific research project they intend to pursue during their residency.

The proposal is a central part of the application and should clearly explain the research project and its relevance to urban problem-solving and city leadership.

The proposal should address several important components.

1. Urban Problem or City Leadership Challenge

Applicants should clearly identify the urban problem or city leadership challenge their research will address.

The problem should be significant and connected to the broader mission of the Bloomberg Center for Cities.

2. Research Questions

The proposal should explain the specific research question or questions that the project will examine.

Applicants should also identify the theory or theories underpinning the work.

3. Research Design and Methodology

Applicants should describe the research design and methodological approach they intend to use.

This should demonstrate how the research questions will be investigated.

4. Significance for Research and Practice

Applicants should explain why the project matters to both:

  • The relevant research field, and
  • The practice of urban problem-solving

The program is particularly interested in work that can contribute not only to scholarship but also to real-world urban challenges.

5. Outputs and Potential Impact

The proposal should also identify the types of outputs envisioned and the potential impact of the research.

Applicants should therefore consider what their research could produce and how those outputs could contribute to scholarship and urban practice.

Selection Process

After applications are submitted, applicants may be invited to participate in an interview with members of a selection committee.

Following the selection process, successful applicants will be formally appointed as Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars.

The selection process therefore considers both the submitted application and, where applicable, the interview stage.

Selection Criteria

Applications will be evaluated based on several key criteria.

Clarity and Significance of the Research Problem

The selection committee will consider how clearly the applicant identifies the research problem and the significance of the issue being studied.

Strength of the Research Design

The quality and strength of the proposed research design will also be considered.

Applicants should clearly explain how their proposed methodology will address their research questions.

Contribution to Scholarship and Practice

The program will assess the potential contribution of the proposed research to:

  • Academic scholarship
  • The practice of urban problem-solving

This reflects the program’s emphasis on research that can have relevance beyond academia.

Alignment With the Bloomberg Center for Cities

Applications will also be evaluated based on their alignment with the mission and thematic interests of the Bloomberg Center for Cities.

Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate how their proposed research connects with the Center’s focus on urban problem-solving and city leadership.

Program Timeline

The application timeline provided for the Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program is:

Stage Date
Application Launch September 16, 2026
Application Deadline October 28, 2026
Notice of Selection February

Applicants should complete and submit their application by October 28, 2026.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Prospective applicants should ensure that their application clearly connects their research with the program’s focus.

1. Define the Urban Challenge Clearly

Start by identifying the specific urban problem or city leadership challenge your research addresses.

2. Develop Clear Research Questions

Make sure the research questions are specific and directly connected to the problem you identify.

3. Explain the Research Methodology

Clearly describe how you intend to conduct the research and why the proposed methodology is appropriate.

4. Demonstrate Relevance to Urban Practice
